cards.t: Tympanometry patterns (types A, B, C, As, Ad)
q: what do the tympanometry types mean
what does a type B tympanogram show
what is a type C tympanogram
how do I read a tympanogram
cards.x:
Tympanometry draws a curve called a tympanogram, and the curve's type tells you what is going on in the middle ear. Each type is judged by where the peak sits (the pressure) and how tall it is (how freely the eardrum moves).

- Type A: normal pressure and normal mobility. Seen in a normal ear, or in sensorineural hearing loss with a normal middle ear.
- Type B: flat, with little or no peak. Seen with fluid in the middle ear, as in acute otitis media or otitis media with effusion.
- Type C: the peak sits at negative pressure (significantly past minus 200 mm of water). Seen in eustachian tube dysfunction.
- Type As: normal pressure but a shallow peak, meaning a stiff system. Seen in otosclerosis or a fixed ossicle (middle ear bone).
- Type Ad: normal pressure but a very tall peak, meaning a floppy system. Seen with a break in the ossicle chain or a flaccid eardrum.

cards.t: Weber and Rinne patterns: normal, conductive and sensorineural loss
q: what do Weber and Rinne show in conductive hearing loss
what do Weber and Rinne show in sensorineural hearing loss
what is a normal Weber and Rinne
what conditions cause each tuning fork pattern
cards.x:
The two tuning fork tests together sort a hearing loss into conductive or sensorineural. Use a 512 hertz fork. For the Weber, put the fork on the top of the head. For the Rinne, put it on the mastoid until the sound fades. Then hold it next to the canal. Compare air conduction (AC, sound through the canal) with bone conduction (BC, sound through the skull).

- Normal: the Weber is midline and equal in both ears, and air conduction is greater than bone conduction.
- Conductive loss: the Weber goes to the bad ear, and bone conduction equals or beats air conduction. Causes include cerumen, otitis media with effusion, acute otitis media, a perforation and otosclerosis.
- Sensorineural loss: the Weber goes to the good ear, and air conduction is still greater than bone conduction. Causes include sudden sensorineural hearing loss, presbycusis, noise, Ménière's disease and acoustic neuroma.

cards.t: Cerumen impaction (earwax blockage)
q: what is cerumen impaction
what are the symptoms of earwax impaction
why does earwax cause hearing loss
what do tuning forks show with wax
cards.x:
Cerumen impaction is earwax that has built up enough to cause symptoms or to block the view of the eardrum. It is the highest-volume ear complaint, and the wax is usually pushed deep by the patient, often while trying to clean the canal with cotton swabs. It also builds up with hearing aids and earbuds, in older adults, and in narrow or hairy canals.

Patients describe muffled hearing (a conductive loss, because the wax blocks sound on its way in), ear fullness and itching; some have ringing in the ear (tinnitus), dizziness or ear pain. Touching the canal can set off a reflex cough through Arnold's nerve, the auricular branch of cranial nerve X. Wax can be wet and sticky, dry and flaky, or dark. With tuning forks, Weber goes to the blocked ear and Rinne shows bone conduction at least as good as air conduction on that side.

Wax only counts as an impaction if it causes symptoms or blocks an exam you need. Look-alike: otitis externa has a swollen canal and pain when the tragus is pressed, not just wax.

cards.t: Removing earwax safely
q: how do you remove earwax safely
when should you not irrigate an ear
why must the eardrum be intact before irrigation
what do you teach patients about cleaning ears
cards.x:
Earwax is removed in two stages: soften it first, then take it out. Softening drops are carbamide peroxide, mineral oil, or plain water or saline. Then there are three ways to get the wax out.

- Irrigation with body-temperature water, only if the eardrum is known to be intact. Water that is too hot or too cold causes caloric vertigo (a spinning sensation).
- A curette or loop, or suction, under direct view. Best for soft wax and a cooperative patient; it can hurt if done wrong.
- If tubes or a perforation (a hole in the drum) are present, the ear, nose and throat specialist does the removal.

If you cannot see the eardrum, you cannot rule out a perforation, so before irrigating ask about tubes, prior ear surgery or a known perforation. Be careful irrigating patients with diabetes or a weakened immune system, because of the risk of malignant otitis externa. Afterward, look at the canal and eardrum again and recheck hearing; if it is still decreased, get audiometry.

Teach that nothing goes in the canal: clean only the opening with a washcloth over a finger. No ear candling.

cards.t: Acute otitis media: what it is and how it looks
q: what is acute otitis media
what does a bulging eardrum mean
what are the signs of a middle ear infection
what bacteria cause ear infections
cards.x:
Acute otitis media is an infection of the middle ear, the space behind the eardrum. It is mostly a childhood problem, peaks around age 2, and usually begins a few days into an upper respiratory infection. Risk factors include daycare, smoke exposure, bottle propping, pacifier use, not being breastfed, enlarged adenoids and allergies.

Patients have ear pain, fever and decreased hearing. Infants tug at the ear and are fussy, with poor sleep or feeding. On exam, the most specific sign is a bulging eardrum, along with redness, loss of the usual landmarks and light reflex, and sometimes visible pus. Pneumatic otoscopy (puffing air against the drum) shows decreased or absent movement. If the drum has ruptured, pus appears in the canal (suppurative otitis media) and the pain often eases. Always check behind the ear for mastoid tenderness or swelling.

The usual bacteria are Streptococcus pneumoniae, nontypeable H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis.

cards.t: How acute otitis media is diagnosed (and told from look-alikes)
q: what are the criteria for acute otitis media
how do you tell acute otitis media from otitis media with effusion
how do you tell otitis media from otitis externa
is tympanometry needed for ear infection
cards.x:
Acute otitis media is a clinical diagnosis. Tympanometry is optional, and it would show a type B curve. The American Academy of Pediatrics criteria always require fluid in the middle ear (an effusion). They also need one of these:

- moderate to severe bulging of the eardrum
- new drainage from the ear that is not from otitis externa
- mild bulging plus ear pain for less than 48 hours, or intense redness

Two look-alikes. Otitis media with effusion is fluid WITHOUT pain, fever or bulging. That distinction decides whether antibiotics are used. Otitis externa causes pain when the tragus (the small flap in front of the ear canal) is pressed, and a swollen canal. If you can see the drum, it is normal. In acute otitis media the canal is normal and the drum bulges.

cards.t: Antibiotics or watchful waiting for acute otitis media
k: when to give antibiotics for otitis media
q: when do you give antibiotics for acute otitis media
what counts as severe otitis media
can you just observe an ear infection
how is ear pain treated in otitis media
cards.x:
Everyone with acute otitis media gets pain control (acetaminophen or ibuprofen), and many cases resolve on their own. Whether to add antibiotics depends on age and severity:

- Under 6 months: antibiotics.
- 6 to 23 months: antibiotics if both ears are affected or it is severe. One ear and not severe: antibiotics or observation.
- 2 years and up: antibiotics if severe. Not severe: antibiotics or observation for 48 to 72 hours with a safety-net plan (a clear plan to come back).

"Severe" means moderate to severe pain, pain lasting 48 hours or more, or a temperature of 39 degrees Celsius (102.2 degrees Fahrenheit) or higher.

cards.t: Antibiotic choice, duration and complications in acute otitis media
q: what is first-line treatment for acute otitis media
what if amoxicillin fails for an ear infection
when do kids need ear tubes
what are the complications of acute otitis media
cards.x:
When antibiotics are used, the first line is high-dose amoxicillin. Switch to amoxicillin-clavulanate if the child had amoxicillin in the last 30 days, has purulent conjunctivitis at the same time (think H. influenzae), or has failed amoxicillin before. With a non-severe penicillin allergy, options include cefdinir, cefuroxime, cefpodoxime or ceftriaxone.

If the child is not better in 48 to 72 hours, re-examine and step up: amoxicillin, then amoxicillin-clavulanate, then ceftriaxone by injection daily for 3 days. Duration: under 2 years or severe is 10 days; ages 2 to 5 is 7 days; age 6 and up is 5 to 7 days.

Recurrent acute otitis media (3 or more episodes in 6 months, or 4 or more in 12 months) or complications call for referral to an ear, nose and throat specialist for tympanostomy tubes. Complications include eardrum perforation, mastoiditis, labyrinthitis and meningitis.

cards.t: Otitis externa (swimmer's ear)
q: what is otitis externa
how do you tell otitis externa from otitis media
what causes swimmer's ear
what is the hallmark of otitis externa
cards.x:
Otitis externa is an infection of the ear canal, the "swimmer's ear". It is most common in kids and teens, and in the summer. Risk factors are swimming or water, humidity, cotton swabs or scratching, anything that plugs the canal (earbuds, hearing aids), skin conditions such as dermatitis or psoriasis, and radiation.

Patients have ear pain that is worse when the ear is touched or moved, plus itching, drainage, fullness and muffled hearing. The hallmark finding is pain when you press on the tragus or pull the auricle (the outer ear). The canal is red and swollen with discharge or debris, and nodes around the ear and in the front of the neck may be enlarged. The eardrum is normal if you can see it, though swelling often hides it.

The number one bacterium is Pseudomonas aeruginosa; others include Staphylococcus epidermidis, Staphylococcus aureus and fungi. It is a clinical diagnosis; culture only if severe, chronic or recurrent, the patient is immunosuppressed, after surgery, or treatment is failing.

cards.t: How otitis externa is treated
q: what is first-line treatment for otitis externa
do you give oral antibiotics for otitis externa
when can you use neomycin ear drops
what is an ear wick for
cards.x:
Topical drops are first line for otitis externa, not oral antibiotics. First, clean out the debris so the drops can reach the canal.

- Fluoroquinolone drops (ciprofloxacin-dexamethasone or ofloxacin) are one option.
- Neomycin, polymyxin B and hydrocortisone drops (Cortisporin) only if the eardrum is intact, because they are ototoxic (harmful to hearing). Neomycin can also cause contact dermatitis.
- If the eardrum is not intact, there are tubes, or you cannot tell: fluoroquinolone drops only.
- Mild cases can use acidifying drops such as acetic acid. Drops with a steroid help with pain and swelling.
- If the canal is too swollen for drops to get in, place an ear wick.

Oral antibiotics are for infection that spreads past the canal, patients with diabetes or a weakened immune system, or when drops cannot be delivered. Also keep the ear dry, give pain control, and recheck if not better in 48 to 72 hours.

cards.t: Teaching a patient to use ear drops
k: how to put in ear drops
q: how do you teach someone to use ear drops
how do you put in ear drops properly
how do you prevent otitis externa
cards.x:
Good drop technique matters because the medicine has to reach the whole canal. Have the patient lie with the affected ear facing up. Fill the canal with drops. Pump the tragus (the small flap in front of the ear canal) to move the drops in. The patient then stays lying down for 3 to 5 minutes.

For prevention, teach patients to dry their ears after swimming and to use acidifying drops. In the exam room, do tragal pressure and the pull on the outer ear before the otoscope goes in. Pain with those two maneuvers is the hallmark of otitis externa.

cards.t: Otomycosis (fungal ear canal infection)
q: what is otomycosis
how do you tell fungal otitis externa from bacterial
what does Aspergillus look like in the ear
how is otomycosis treated
cards.x:
Otomycosis is a fungal infection of the ear canal. The clue is that it itches more than it hurts, and you can see fungal threads (hyphae) or debris. Aspergillus looks like black or gray spores, often described as "wet newspaper". Candida looks like white, fluffy, curd-like material.

Compare ordinary bacterial otitis externa, where pain with tragal pressure dominates and the canal is swollen.

Treatment is to clean the canal out and use a topical antifungal such as clotrimazole solution.

cards.t: Otitis media with effusion (fluid behind the eardrum)
q: what is otitis media with effusion
how is otitis media with effusion different from acute otitis media
what does the eardrum look like with fluid behind it
what are the complications of ear fluid
cards.x:
Otitis media with effusion is fluid behind the eardrum with no acute infection. It is often left over after acute otitis media. The big contrast: there is no pain and no fever. Patients have muffled hearing and fullness, or no symptoms at all and it is found on otoscopy. In children it may show up as speech or language delay, not paying attention, or trouble in school.

On exam the drum is dull (amber, yellow or gray), often retracted, with an air-fluid level or bubbles. Movement is decreased on pneumatic otoscopy, and there is no bulging and no real redness. Weber goes to the affected ear and Rinne shows bone conduction at least as good as air conduction. Tympanometry shows type B.

Compare eustachian tube dysfunction, which is retraction without fluid, and acute otitis media, which has pain, fever and bulging. Complications are temporary conductive hearing loss, speech delay and acquired cholesteatoma.

cards.t: Managing otitis media with effusion
q: do you treat otitis media with effusion with antibiotics
when do kids with ear fluid need tubes
what do you do for otitis media with effusion
when is a hearing test needed for ear fluid
cards.x:
Most cases of otitis media with effusion clear up on their own, so the plan is watchful waiting with a recheck about every 3 months. Do not use antibiotics, steroids, antihistamines or decongestants: they do not clear the fluid.

A hearing test is done if the fluid lasts 3 months or more, or the child is at risk for speech or learning problems. If it lasts 3 months or more with hearing loss or speech concerns, refer to an ear, nose and throat specialist for tympanostomy tubes. Adenoidectomy (removing the adenoids) is added if big adenoids are blocking the eustachian tube.

In the exam room, a good one-line summary is "no pain, no fever, no bulging."

cards.t: One-sided ear fluid in an adult (the red flag)
q: why is one-sided ear fluid in an adult worrying
what should you do for an adult with persistent unilateral ear fluid
who is at risk for nasopharyngeal carcinoma
cards.x:
An adult with fluid in one ear that won't go away is a red flag. The worry is a nasopharyngeal carcinoma, a cancer at the back of the nose that blocks the eustachian tube, so fluid builds up behind the drum.

The next step is nasopharyngoscopy (looking at the back of the nose with a scope) to rule out a nasopharyngeal mass. The risk is higher in people of Southern Chinese or Southeast Asian descent, and the cancer is linked to Epstein-Barr virus.

cards.t: Eustachian tube dysfunction
q: what is eustachian tube dysfunction
why does my ear feel full after a cold
what does the eardrum look like in eustachian tube dysfunction
how do you tell eustachian tube dysfunction from otitis media with effusion
cards.x:
In eustachian tube dysfunction the eustachian tube is swollen shut, so the middle ear cannot equalize its pressure. It usually follows a cold or allergies and lasts days to weeks.

Patients have fullness, mild to moderate muffled hearing, and crackling or popping with swallowing or yawning. It is worse with altitude changes (flying, mountains), diving and a cold. The eardrum is retracted. The short process of the malleus (one of the middle ear bones) stands out, the handle looks shortened, and movement is decreased. Tympanometry shows type C (negative pressure), or type B if fluid has built up.

Compare otitis media with effusion, which has amber fluid or a visible level behind the drum rather than just retraction. Also compare cerumen impaction, where wax blocks the canal so the drum cannot be seen at all.

cards.t: Ear barotrauma (flying and diving injuries)
q: what is ear barotrauma
why does my ear hurt when flying or diving
what is a perilymph fistula
when does barotrauma need urgent referral
cards.x:
Barotrauma is ear injury from pressure changes, when the eustachian tube cannot equalize pressure. Patients have ear pain (usually on descent) and conductive hearing loss after flying or diving. It can cause bleeding into the middle ear (hemotympanum), an effusion, or an eardrum rupture.

Inner ear symptoms change the picture: vertigo, tinnitus, sensorineural hearing loss, or nausea and vomiting suggest a tear in the round or oval window, called a perilymph fistula. Any inner ear symptoms, and especially a sensorineural hearing pattern after a dive or flight, mean urgent referral to an ear, nose and throat specialist.

With an intact eardrum but severe pain and hearing loss, the specialist may do a myringotomy (a small cut in the eardrum). A perforation should be kept dry and most heal on their own over several weeks.

cards.t: Treating eustachian tube dysfunction and flying with it
q: how do you treat eustachian tube dysfunction
how can I pop my ears safely
how should someone fly with eustachian tube dysfunction
why limit oxymetazoline to 3 days
cards.x:
First treat the cause: intranasal steroids, and short-term oral or nasal decongestants (oxymetazoline for no more than 3 days).

Autoinflation means exhaling against a closed nose, swallowing, yawning or chewing gum to open the tube. Use caution with active nasal discharge, since the pressure can push infected mucus into the middle ear and cause acute otitis media.

Avoid flying or diving until it clears. If the patient must fly: a decongestant beforehand, and swallowing and yawning on descent; infants should feed during descent. Frequent flyers with repeated episodes may need tubes. In the room, ask about recent flights, diving and a recent cold or allergy flare, and describe the drum as retracted, not bulging.

cards.t: Sensorineural hearing loss (what it is and how it presents)
q: what is sensorineural hearing loss
how does sensorineural hearing loss present
how do you tell sensorineural from conductive hearing loss on exam
why is tinnitus a red flag
cards.x:
Sensorineural hearing loss is a problem in the cochlea (its hair cells) or in cranial nerve VIII and beyond. It is usually not fixable. But it can often be stabilized, some causes are preventable, and sudden loss may respond to steroids in the first weeks.

Patients say "people mumble". They struggle in groups or crowded rooms, on the phone or with the TV, and the partner complains. Hearing is worse in background noise, and the patient may talk loudly (conductive loss is the opposite). Ringing in the ears (tinnitus) is often the first symptom. One-sided or pulsatile tinnitus is a red flag. Gradual loss in both ears suggests presbycusis, noise or ototoxic (ear-damaging) drugs. Sudden loss in one ear is a different problem.

On exam the canal and eardrum are normal (wax or fluid would mean conductive loss). The Weber goes to the good ear, and the Rinne shows air conduction better than bone conduction.

cards.t: What to ask in sensorineural hearing loss
q: what do you ask about with sensorineural hearing loss
which drugs damage hearing
what history points to a cause of hearing loss
cards.x:
The history looks for the cause, so ask about:

- noise exposure (job, firearms, concerts)
- ototoxic medications (aminoglycosides, furosemide, aspirin, platinum chemotherapy)
- head trauma
- episodes of spinning vertigo, or a recent upper respiratory infection with vertigo
- a "pop" with flying, diving or straining
- family history, and autoimmune disease
- sexually transmitted infection or HIV risk, and diabetes or vascular disease
- facial numbness or weakness, and imbalance

Some of these answers point to a specific cause: a "pop" is a clue to a perilymph fistula, and facial numbness or weakness with imbalance can point to an acoustic neuroma.

cards.t: Testing sensorineural hearing loss
q: how is sensorineural hearing loss tested
what are the degrees of hearing loss in decibels
when do you order magnetic resonance imaging for hearing loss
do you need labs for hearing loss
cards.x:
Pure tone audiometry confirms the type and severity of the loss. Severity bands: normal 0 to 20 decibels, mild 20 to 40, moderate 40 to 60, severe 60 to 80, profound above 80. Tympanometry shows type A, meaning the middle ear is fine.

Speech discrimination (understanding words) that is worse than the tone loss predicts makes you think of acoustic neuroma. One-sided or asymmetric sensorineural loss gets magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with gadolinium, the gold standard for retrocochlear causes (problems behind the cochlea). Vestibular testing is added if there is vertigo, or one-sided loss with balance symptoms.

Labs are not routine. The exception is syphilis: use the fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption test or the microhemagglutination assay for Treponema pallidum, because the Venereal Disease Research Laboratory test is not helpful. Test for HIV if there are risk factors.

cards.t: Treating and living with sensorineural hearing loss
q: how is sensorineural hearing loss treated
when is a cochlear implant considered
how do you treat tinnitus
how should family talk to someone with hearing loss
cards.x:
The approach is to treat or remove the cause when you can. Otherwise, stabilize and amplify. That means hearing aids, and cochlear implant evaluation for severe to profound loss.

Prevention: hearing protection and avoiding loud noise, monitoring aminoglycoside levels, and stopping or changing ototoxic drugs together with the prescriber. Sudden loss gets oral steroids and urgent referral to an ear, nose and throat specialist.

Tinnitus can be managed with masking noise or biofeedback. No drug has beaten placebo. Tips for family: face the patient, speak slowly and clearly, and cut background noise. In the exam room, look in the ear first so you can say "the canal and eardrum are normal". Then name the tuning fork pattern out loud and order an audiogram.

cards.t: Presbycusis (age-related hearing loss)
k: high frequency hearing loss in elderly
q: what is presbycusis
what are the features of presbycusis
why can older adults hear but not understand speech
cards.x:
Presbycusis is the hearing loss of aging. It affects older adults gradually, in both ears and symmetrically, and it takes the high pitches first.

The classic story is that the patient hears people talking but cannot make out the words, and misses the doorbell or the phone. The audiogram confirms it, and the treatment is hearing aids.

cards.t: Noise-induced hearing loss
q: what is noise-induced hearing loss
what does the audiogram show in noise-induced hearing loss
is noise-induced hearing loss permanent
how do you prevent noise-induced hearing loss
cards.x:
Noise-induced hearing loss comes from loud exposure at a job, from guns or at concerts. After a single loud exposure, people may feel full ears and hear "crickets"; this temporary shift recovers in 24 to 48 hours. Repeated exposure leads to permanent loss.

The audiogram classically shows a notch around 4,000 hertz. It is diagnosed with an audiogram, and prevention is hearing protection.

cards.t: Ototoxic drugs and hearing loss
q: which drugs cause hearing loss
what is ototoxicity
what do you do when a drug is damaging hearing
cards.x:
Ototoxicity means a drug damages hearing. The aminoglycosides are the most common cause. Others are loop diuretics (such as furosemide), aspirin, and platinum chemotherapy.

The loss affects both ears, and these drugs are often nephrotoxic too, meaning they can harm the kidneys as well. Treatment is to stop or adjust the drug together with the prescriber, and to monitor aminoglycoside levels.

cards.t: Ménière's disease
q: what is Ménière's disease
what are the symptoms of Ménière's disease
how does Ménière's differ from other causes of vertigo
cards.x:
Ménière's disease is an inner ear problem with a recognizable cluster: spinning vertigo lasting hours, fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss, a low "blowing" tinnitus, and one-sided ear fullness. Nausea and vomiting come with the spinning.

The key word is fluctuating: the hearing loss comes and goes, especially in the low pitches. Workup is an audiogram, and the patient is referred to an ear, nose and throat specialist. Syphilis and HIV can look just like Ménière's.

cards.t: Acoustic neuroma
q: what is an acoustic neuroma
how do you diagnose an acoustic neuroma
why does an acoustic neuroma cause poor speech understanding
cards.x:
An acoustic neuroma is a growth on the nerve of hearing and balance. Think of it with one-sided, progressive hearing loss (it can be sudden), tinnitus, imbalance, and especially poor speech understanding: speech discrimination is worse than the pure tone loss predicts. It may involve cranial nerves V and VII, causing facial numbness or weakness.

Magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium is the test, and the gold standard for retrocochlear causes. Treatment is observation with yearly magnetic resonance imaging, surgery or radiation.

cards.t: Labyrinthitis and perilymph fistula
q: what is labyrinthitis
how does a perilymph fistula present
how is labyrinthitis treated
cards.x:
Two causes of sensorineural loss that come with vertigo:

- Labyrinthitis: fairly sudden sensorineural hearing loss plus acute vertigo, usually viral. Treat with symptom care, oral steroids, and meclizine or diazepam for the acute vertigo; antibiotics if it is bacterial.
- Perilymph fistula: sensorineural loss plus vertigo after head injury, barotrauma (pressure injury) or heavy straining, sometimes with a "pop". Treat with symptom care and refer to an ear, nose and throat specialist.

The history separates them: a recent viral illness fits labyrinthitis, while an injury or a pressure event fits a fistula.

cards.t: Other causes of sensorineural loss: syphilis, HIV, autoimmune
q: can syphilis cause hearing loss
what is autoimmune hearing loss
what looks like Ménière's disease but is not
cards.x:
Syphilis and HIV can cause fluctuating sensorineural loss with tinnitus, fullness and episodic vertigo, so they can look just like Ménière's disease. Test with a fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption test or the microhemagglutination assay for Treponema pallidum, and an HIV test. Treat syphilis with antibiotics plus systemic steroids.

Autoimmune loss affects both ears and is progressive with ups and downs, sometimes with balance problems. It is managed by an ear, nose and throat specialist or a rheumatologist, and there is no routine autoimmune screening.

cards.t: Mastoiditis (a complication of ear infection)
q: what is mastoiditis
how does mastoiditis present
how do you treat mastoiditis
how do you tell mastoiditis from otitis media
cards.x:
Mastoiditis is a complication of acute otitis media in which the infection spreads into the mastoid air cells, the bone behind the ear. It is mostly seen in kids, with a recent or current ear infection plus pain behind the ear and fever.

Look behind the ear for redness, swelling, tenderness or fluctuance (a fluid-filled, soft area). The auricle is pushed forward and out, and the crease behind the ear is gone. The eardrum usually looks like acute otitis media. Uncomplicated acute otitis media has no swelling behind the ear or protruding auricle, and postauricular lymphadenitis is a discrete mobile node with the auricle in place.

Order computed tomography (CT) of the temporal bone with contrast, blood tests and cultures. Treatment is admission, intravenous antibiotics and an ear, nose and throat specialist (myringotomy, with mastoidectomy for an abscess or if there is no improvement). Watch for meningitis, sigmoid sinus thrombosis, brain abscess and facial nerve palsy.

cards.t: Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa
q: what is malignant otitis externa
who gets malignant otitis externa
how do you tell it from ordinary otitis externa
how is malignant otitis externa treated
cards.x:
Malignant otitis externa is a severe ear canal infection that invades bone. Suspect it in an elderly diabetic or immunocompromised patient whose "otitis externa" won't get better. Pseudomonas causes more than 95 percent of cases.

The pain is out of proportion to the exam, often worse at night, with heavy drainage. Look for granulation tissue on the floor of the canal, visible necrosis, and facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) weakness; later cranial nerves IX, X and XI. Ordinary otitis externa responds to drops within days and has no granulation or night pain.

Computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging shows infection in the bone and skull base. Blood inflammation markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein) are high and are used to follow treatment. Biopsy rules out canal carcinoma, which looks similar and also fails treatment. Management is ear, nose and throat care, usually admission, a long course of antipseudomonal antibiotics (typically 6 to 8 weeks), tight glucose control and debridement.

cards.t: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss: how to recognize it
k: sudden hearing loss in one ear
woke up deaf in one ear
q: what is sudden sensorineural hearing loss
how do you recognize sudden hearing loss
why is sudden hearing loss mistaken for wax
what does Weber show in sudden hearing loss
cards.x:
Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is hearing loss in one ear that comes on over 72 hours or less. Patients often notice it on waking or on the phone, with fullness, tinnitus, and sometimes vertigo. It is easy to mistake for wax or fluid, so actually look in the ear. It is a syndrome, not a single disease (viral or vascular causes), and it needs prompt referral to an ear, nose and throat specialist.

The otoscopy is normal. Weber goes to the good ear and Rinne shows air conduction better than bone. Vertigo plus neurologic deficits means think stroke.

Cerumen impaction has visible wax and Weber goes toward the blocked ear; otitis media with effusion has an amber, poorly moving drum and a conductive pattern.

cards.t: Managing sudden sensorineural hearing loss
q: how do you treat sudden hearing loss
how fast must steroids be started for sudden hearing loss
what tests are needed for sudden hearing loss
cards.x:
Treat as an urgent problem. Get audiometry as soon as possible to confirm sensorineural loss, and magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium to rule out acoustic neuroma. Routine labs are not needed, except syphilis testing; consider an HIV test if there are risk factors. No routine head computed tomography.

Start oral steroids right away (prednisone for 7 to 14 days, then a taper). Steroids help most in the first couple of weeks; after that the window closes. Arrange urgent referral to an ear, nose and throat specialist. Salvage options are intratympanic steroid injections (into the middle ear) and hyperbaric oxygen. Repeat audiometry, and evaluate for hearing aids or a cochlear implant if recovery is incomplete.

A model line for the exam: "This came on suddenly in one ear with a normal ear exam, so I'm treating it as sudden sensorineural loss: audiogram today, prednisone now, urgent referral and a magnetic resonance imaging scan with gadolinium."

cards.t: Telling the common ear conditions apart
k: AOM vs OME vs OE vs ETD
q: how do you tell acute otitis media from otitis externa
how do you tell otitis media from eustachian tube dysfunction
which ear conditions need antibiotics
cards.x:
Four common conditions differ on a few quick features. In order, they are acute otitis media, otitis media with effusion, otitis externa and eustachian tube dysfunction.

- Pain: yes; no; yes and worse moving the ear; pressure or mild pain.
- Fever: often; no; usually no; no.
- Pain with tragus or auricle pressure: only otitis externa.
- Eardrum: red and bulging with landmarks gone; dull amber with an air-fluid level; normal if seen but the canal is swollen; retracted.
- Mobility: decreased or absent; decreased; normal; decreased.
- Tympanogram: type B; type B; type A if tolerated; type C.
- Antibiotics: oral or observe; no; topical drops; no.

So the two conditions with a type B curve are the two fluid conditions. Only one of them, acute otitis media, is a true infection that may need oral antibiotics.

cards.t: The common cold (viral rhinitis)
q: what is viral rhinitis
does green mucus mean a bacterial infection
how long does a cold last
how do you tell a cold from allergic rhinitis
cards.x:
The common cold is a viral upper respiratory infection, and 90 to 98 percent of acute rhinosinusitis is viral, not bacterial. Rhinovirus is the most common cause.

It starts with a scratchy throat, then congestion, sneezing and a clear runny nose that can turn thick and yellow or green. Color alone does not mean bacterial. Symptoms peak on days 3 to 5 and improve by days 7 to 10, though a cough can hang on longer. A low-grade fever is possible, more so in kids. The nasal lining is red and swollen (pale and boggy in allergies), and facial pain is not reproducible on palpation the way it is in bacterial sinusitis.

Compare allergic rhinitis: lots of itching and sneezing, pale bluish boggy lining, no fever, and a seasonal or trigger-linked pattern. Compare acute bacterial rhinosinusitis: purulence with tender, often one-sided facial pain. No test reliably separates viral from bacterial.

cards.t: Treating the common cold
q: how do you treat a cold
why limit decongestant spray to 3 days
do you give antibiotics for a cold
when should a patient with a cold come back
cards.x:
Antibiotics do not help a cold, because it is viral. Treatment is supportive: fluids, rest, saline spray or irrigation, and acetaminophen or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).

Decongestants can be used short term, with caution in patients with high blood pressure. Oxymetazoline should be used for no more than 3 days, because longer use can cause rebound congestion, called rhinitis medicamentosa. Intranasal ipratropium helps a runny nose. Honey helps a cough (not under age 1), and over-the-counter cough and cold medicines should be avoided in young kids. For influenza, oseltamivir for 5 days is the antiviral.

Tell patients the timeline in plain words: it should peak in 3 to 5 days and be better by 7 to 10. Come back if it lasts past 10 days, gets better and then worse, brings a high fever, or causes eye swelling.

cards.t: Allergic rhinitis: what it is and how it looks
q: what is allergic rhinitis
what does the nose look like in allergic rhinitis
how do you tell allergic rhinitis from a cold
what is the allergic salute
cards.x:
Allergic rhinitis is an immunoglobulin E (IgE) reaction to an allergen. It is very common and increasing, and the diagnosis is mostly the history.

Patients have sneezing fits, an itchy nose, eyes and palate, a clear watery runny nose, congestion and itchy watery eyes, with no fever. It may be seasonal (pollen) or year-round (dust mites, pets, mold). So timing and triggers are the key history. Asthma or eczema in the patient or family is common. On exam the turbinates (shelf-like structures on the side wall of the nose) are pale or bluish and boggy (swollen), with clear discharge from both sides. Sometimes there are nasal polyps. Other signs are allergic shiners, Dennie-Morgan lines, a transverse nasal crease (the "allergic salute"), red eyes, and cobblestoning of the back of the throat.

A cold lasts days rather than a season, comes with a sore throat and has no itch. Vasomotor rhinitis is triggered by temperature, odors and food, with no itch or sneezing fits.

cards.t: Testing in allergic rhinitis
q: do you need allergy testing for allergic rhinitis
when do you image allergic rhinitis
why test kids with nasal polyps for cystic fibrosis
cards.x:
Allergic rhinitis is a clinical diagnosis, so most patients need no testing. Allergy testing (a skin prick or a blood test for specific immunoglobulin E) is used when the diagnosis is unclear, treatment isn't working, or to guide avoidance or immunotherapy. There is no imaging for routine allergic rhinitis.

If nasal polyps are present, the workup adds a blood count with differential and immunoglobulin E. In kids with polyps, a sweat chloride test looks for cystic fibrosis.

cards.t: Treating allergic rhinitis
q: what is the best treatment for allergic rhinitis
which allergy medicine works best
is montelukast first line for allergies
how do you avoid allergy triggers
cards.x:
Most patients (80 percent) end up on two or more allergy medicines. Start with avoiding triggers: allergen-proof bedding covers, a HEPA (high-efficiency particulate air) filter, pets out of the bedroom, and windows closed during pollen season.

- An intranasal steroid (fluticasone, mometasone, budesonide) is the most effective single drug. Aim away from the septum; the full effect takes days to weeks.
- A second-generation oral antihistamine (loratadine, fexofenadine, cetirizine, levocetirizine; cetirizine and levocetirizine can still cause some sleepiness) treats sneezing and itch; the drowsy older ones can be tried at night.
- An intranasal antihistamine (azelastine) works fast and can be combined with the nasal steroid for moderate to severe symptoms.
- Intranasal ipratropium treats a runny nose.
- A leukotriene inhibitor (montelukast) is not first line, and it carries a boxed warning for mood and behavior effects. It is most useful if asthma is also present.

Decongestants are short term only. Immunotherapy (shots or under-the-tongue tablets) is for patients not controlled, and eye drops help eye symptoms.

cards.t: Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis: when is a sinus infection bacterial?
q: when is sinusitis bacterial
what is double worsening
how long do sinus symptoms last before antibiotics
what are the symptoms of bacterial sinusitis
cards.x:
Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis is a sinus infection lasting less than 4 weeks. Only 0.5 to 2 percent of viral cases turn bacterial, so the skill is spotting the pattern. Patients have purulent (pus-like) nasal drainage plus congestion and/or facial pain or pressure. The pain or pressure is worse bending over or lying down. They may also have upper tooth pain, bad breath, decreased smell, headache, ear pain or cough.

Call it bacterial when you see one of three patterns:

- Persistent: 10 days or more without improvement.
- Severe onset: a fever of 39 degrees Celsius (102 degrees Fahrenheit) or higher with purulent discharge or facial pain for 3 to 4 days in a row at the start.
- Double worsening: gets better, then worse again after day 5 or 6.

Risk factors are allergies, smoking, a weakened immune system, and anatomic problems such as a deviated septum. A viral illness, by contrast, peaks early in the first week and then improves, with no double worsening.

cards.t: Examining and working up a sinus infection
q: do you need imaging for sinusitis
what do you look for on exam in sinusitis
when do you get a CT for sinusitis
why check the eyes in sinusitis
cards.x:
Acute sinusitis is a clinical diagnosis. On exam look for purulent discharge, swollen nasal lining and sinus tenderness (often one-sided over the maxillary sinus). Confirm any fever yourself and make sure the patient didn't take a fever reducer first. Check the eyes (swelling, eye movements, vision) and mental status every time, because that is how complications show up.

There is no routine imaging, because X-rays and computed tomography (CT) cannot tell viral from bacterial. Sinus computed tomography is for when sinusitis keeps coming back, treatment fails, a complication of the eye or brain is suspected, or it is chronic. In children the usual bacteria are Streptococcus pneumoniae, nontypeable H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis.

In the room, pin down the timeline out loud ("How many days has it been? Did you get better and then worse?") and say you would not image unless you suspected a complication.

cards.t: Treating acute bacterial sinusitis
q: how do you treat bacterial sinusitis
what antibiotic is used for sinusitis
how long are antibiotics given for sinusitis
can you watch and wait with sinusitis
cards.x:
Everyone gets symptom care: saline irrigation (a Neti pot with distilled or boiled water), intranasal steroids, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and short-term decongestants.

Antibiotics are for bacterial sinusitis. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is the usual first choice. The adult sinusitis guideline from the ear, nose and throat society also allows amoxicillin with or without clavulanate. Adults with reliable follow-up can choose watchful waiting instead. If the patient has had antibiotics in the last 30 days or resistance is high, use the extended-release amoxicillin-clavulanate. With a penicillin allergy, options are doxycycline or moxifloxacin. Avoid macrolides because of resistance.

Duration is 5 to 7 days for adults and 10 to 14 days for kids. If medical treatment fails, refer to an ear, nose and throat specialist. Chronic sinusitis (over 12 weeks) calls for sinus computed tomography, referral, and allergy testing.

cards.t: Epistaxis: anterior versus posterior nosebleeds and their causes
q: what is epistaxis
where do most nosebleeds come from
how do you tell anterior from posterior epistaxis
what causes nosebleeds
cards.x:
Epistaxis is a nosebleed. It peaks in kids under 10 and adults 45 to 65, and is more common in winter. About 90 percent are anterior, coming from Kiesselbach's plexus on the front of the septum. Posterior bleeds usually come from branches of the sphenopalatine artery. They are heavier and carry a higher risk of aspiration (blood going into the airway). Blood running down the back of the throat, or bleeding from both sides, makes you think posterior.

The most common cause is the patient's own finger, and a chronic dry nose is a risk factor. Other causes are trauma, recent surgery, intranasal steroids and cocaine. Medicines that raise the risk include warfarin, aspirin, clopidogrel and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Also think of bleeding disorders, cirrhosis, HIV and tumors. Ask about symptoms of blood loss (lightheaded, chest pain, short of breath), especially in coronary artery disease or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (long-term lung disease). Start with the airway, breathing, circulation and vital signs.

cards.t: Stopping a nosebleed: the pinch steps
q: how do you stop a nosebleed
where do you pinch for a nosebleed
should you lean forward or back for a nosebleed
what home care helps prevent nosebleeds
cards.x:
Stopping a nosebleed starts with three first-line steps:

1. Sit up and lean forward at the waist, and spit out blood instead of swallowing it.
2. Blow out the clots, then spray oxymetazoline.
3. Pinch the soft part of the nose against the septum continuously for 10 minutes, no peeking. A cold compress on the bridge can help.

Pinch the soft part of the nose, not the bony bridge. Teach the patient the technique for next time. Prevention and home care: a humidifier, saline spray, petroleum jelly inside the nose, trimmed nails, and no picking. After packing, no nose blowing.

cards.t: When pinching fails: cautery, packing and testing
q: how do you treat a nosebleed that won't stop
why cauterize only one side of the septum
when is a nosebleed admitted
what labs are needed for a nosebleed
cards.x:
If pinching fails and you can see an anterior bleeding spot, use silver nitrate cautery after topical anesthetic. Cauterize only one side of the septum, since both sides can cause a septal perforation (a hole in the septum).

Still bleeding means packing: a nasal tampon, gauze, a balloon catheter, or clotting foam or gel. A posterior bleed needs posterior packing or a balloon, admission, and referral to an ear, nose and throat specialist. Don't automatically stop anticoagulants for a bleed you have controlled; talk with the prescriber.

Most patients need no labs. Check prothrombin time and the international normalized ratio (blood clotting tests) only if the patient is anticoagulated. For a massive or prolonged bleed, get a hematocrit, type and crossmatch, and two large-bore intravenous lines. Pursue a clotting workup if a bleeding disorder is suspected, and computed tomography or endoscopy if you suspect a mass or recurrent posterior bleeding.

cards.t: Nasal foreign body in a child
q: what does a nasal foreign body look like
why is one-sided foul discharge in a toddler a foreign body
where do nasal foreign bodies get stuck
how do you tell nasal foreign body from sinusitis
cards.x:
Nasal foreign bodies are mostly seen in young kids. The one-liner to remember: unilateral, purulent, foul-smelling discharge in a young child is a foreign body until proven otherwise. Often nobody saw it happen. The objects can be beads, food, toy parts, paper, button batteries or magnets, and the child has one-sided stuffiness and foul, purulent, maybe bloody discharge.

Look with an otoscope or headlight; seeing it makes the diagnosis. Usual spots are the nasal floor just under the inferior turbinate, or up high in front of the middle turbinate. Check the other nostril and both ears too, since kids who put one thing in often put in more. Imaging is rarely needed, but get an X-ray if a metal object is possible or unknown.

Look-alikes: unilateral sinusitis (discharge without an object, far less common at this age) and choanal atresia (congenital, present from birth, with a blocked side and mucus-like rather than foul discharge). In the room, specifically ask about batteries and magnets.

cards.t: Button batteries and magnets in the nose
q: why is a button battery in the nose an emergency
what does a button battery look like on X-ray
why are magnets in the nose dangerous
cards.x:
A button battery in the nose is an emergency. It burns through tissue within hours and can perforate the septum, so it needs emergent removal by an ear, nose and throat specialist. Don't put saline drops in first. On a front-view X-ray, a button battery shows a "double ring".

Magnets on both sides of the septum are just as urgent, because the pressure causes necrosis (tissue death). Ask specifically about batteries and magnets in any child with a suspected nasal foreign body.

cards.t: Removing a nasal foreign body
q: how do you remove a nasal foreign body
what is the parent's kiss technique
why not irrigate beans out of the nose
when do you refer a nasal foreign body
cards.x:
Removing a nasal foreign body starts with preparation. Use oxymetazoline, with or without topical lidocaine, and hold the child still (papoose) or sedate if needed. Try positive pressure first: the "parent's kiss". Block the clear nostril and the parent gives a quick puff into the child's mouth. Older kids can blow with the clear side blocked.

If that fails, use instruments:

- alligator forceps for soft or graspable things
- a right-angle hook or curette behind round or hard things
- a balloon catheter passed behind the object and pulled forward
- suction

Don't push the object backward (aspiration risk). Don't irrigate organic items such as beans, because they swell. After removal, recheck both sides for injury or a second object.

Refer to an ear, nose and throat specialist if any of these apply: the object is posterior or stuck, an attempt failed, it is a battery or magnet, or there is significant tissue damage.

cards.t: One-sided nasal obstruction or bleeding in an adult: think tumor
q: why is one-sided nasal obstruction in an adult worrying
what is juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma
should a unilateral nasal polyp be biopsied
cards.x:
In an adult, one-sided stuffiness or repeated one-sided nosebleeds is tumor until proven otherwise. Other clues are one-sided ear fluid, facial numbness, double vision, headache or a neck mass. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is common in Southern China, Southeast Asia, North Africa, the Middle East and the Arctic. It affects men 2 to 3 times more than women. It is linked to Epstein-Barr virus, human papillomavirus, smoking and salty diets.

A teen boy with one-sided obstruction and heavy nosebleeds suggests juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma, a very vascular (full of blood vessels) tumor, so don't biopsy it in clinic. A one-sided "simple polyp" isn't always simple. An inverted papilloma can harbor carcinoma.

Examine for a one-sided mass or polyp. Check cranial nerves V and VI, the eyes, both ears for fluid, and the neck nodes. Refer promptly to an ear, nose and throat specialist for nasal endoscopy with a guided biopsy, plus imaging.

cards.t: Sinusitis spreading to the eye: preseptal versus orbital cellulitis
q: how do you tell preseptal from orbital cellulitis
what are the signs of orbital cellulitis
what are warning signs of sinusitis complications
how is orbital cellulitis treated
cards.x:
Sinusitis can spread to the orbit (the eye socket); the ethmoid sinuses are the classic source in kids. The urgent warning signs are vision changes (especially double vision), swelling or redness around the eye, and altered mental status.

The key is separating two things:

- Preseptal cellulitis: red, swollen eyelid, but vision, eye movements and pupils are normal, there is no pain moving the eye and no proptosis (bulging eye).
- Orbital (post-septal) cellulitis: proptosis, pain with eye movement, limited movement or double vision, decreased vision, chemosis (swelling of the conjunctiva) and an afferent pupillary defect.

Both eyes involved plus cranial nerve palsies and a toxic patient suggests cavernous sinus thrombosis; headache, stiff neck and confusion suggest spread into the head. Get computed tomography of the orbits and sinuses with contrast. Orbital cellulitis means admission, intravenous antibiotics and urgent eye and ear, nose and throat care; mild preseptal cellulitis in a reliable patient can be treated orally with a recheck next day.

cards.t: Invasive fungal sinusitis
q: what is invasive fungal sinusitis
who gets invasive fungal sinusitis
what does mucormycosis look like in the nose
cards.x:
Think of invasive fungal sinusitis (Mucor, Rhizopus) in an immunocompromised patient or one with diabetic ketoacidosis who has sinus symptoms. The sign to look for is a black eschar (dead, blackened tissue) on the turbinate or palate.

It is an emergency: treatment is surgical debridement plus intravenous amphotericin B.

cards.t: Telling cold, allergic rhinitis and bacterial sinusitis apart
k: viral vs allergic vs bacterial rhinitis
q: how do you tell a cold from allergies from sinusitis
how does discharge differ in allergic rhinitis and sinusitis
which nasal condition gets antibiotics
cards.x:
Three common nose conditions can be told apart by a few features. In order: viral rhinitis (cold), allergic rhinitis, bacterial sinusitis.

- Discharge: clear and can turn colored; clear and watery; purulent.
- Itch and sneezing: some sneezing; lots; none.
- Fever: low-grade early; none; can be high with a severe onset.
- Nasal lining: red and swollen; pale and bluish, boggy; red with purulent drainage.
- Facial pain: minimal and not reproducible; pressure only; yes, often one-sided and tender.
- Timeline: peaks day 3 to 5 and better by 7 to 10; seasonal or trigger-linked and recurring; 10 days or more, severe onset, or double worsening.
- Treatment: supportive; nasal steroid with or without an antihistamine; amoxicillin-clavulanate (or watchful waiting).

cards.t: Viral pharyngitis
q: how do you recognize a viral sore throat
what clues point to a virus in pharyngitis
how is viral pharyngitis treated
which sore throat symptom argues against strep
cards.x:
About 70 percent of pharyngitis is viral. Patients have a sore throat plus cough, runny nose, hoarseness, conjunctivitis (pink eye), ear pain or headache. Cough is the most useful sign against strep. The pharynx is red, with perhaps a little exudate, red eyes, a runny nose and maybe nodes.

Clues to the specific virus: adenovirus (pink eye plus sore throat), coxsackie (herpangina: vesicles or ulcers on the tonsils and soft palate), herpes simplex (gingivostomatitis), Epstein-Barr virus (mono), and acute HIV (sexual risk, rash, ulcers).

Compare strep: exudate, tender anterior nodes, fever and no cough. Mono: posterior nodes, marked fatigue, a big spleen and palatal petechiae.

Diagnosis is clinical, with no strep test when viral features are obvious. Treatment is supportive (fluids, rest, acetaminophen, gargles, lozenges) with no antibiotics. Avoid benzocaine sprays in children under 2 because of methemoglobinemia. Return for drooling, inability to open the mouth, a muffled voice, inability to swallow, trouble breathing or one-sided swelling.

cards.t: Group A strep pharyngitis (strep throat)
q: what is group A strep pharyngitis
how do you recognize strep throat
what is scarlet fever
how do you tell strep throat from a viral sore throat
cards.x:
Group A strep pharyngitis is a throat infection with Streptococcus pyogenes. It is seen in kids and teens (not usually under 3), in winter and spring, spreads by droplets, and has an incubation of 2 to 5 days.

The onset is sudden: sore throat, fever above 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit, painful swallowing, no cough, and abdominal pain; kids may also have headache and nausea. Scarlet fever adds a sandpaper rash and a strawberry tongue. On exam the tonsils and pharynx are red with purulent exudate and the anterior neck nodes are tender; look for palatal petechiae and a swollen uvula.

Viral pharyngitis comes with cough, coryza (runny nose) and hoarseness, and has a low Centor score. Infectious mononucleosis has POSTERIOR nodes and a big spleen, and giving amoxicillin to a mono patient causes a rash.

cards.t: The Centor score (with age points)
q: what is the Centor score
what are the Centor criteria
how do you use the Centor score to decide on testing
what age points does the modified Centor score add
cards.x:
The Centor score is a point system that helps decide who needs a strep test. Each of these scores one point: fever above 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit, tonsillar exudate or swelling, tender anterior cervical nodes, and no cough. Three are things present and one is a thing absent, so the missing cough is the one people forget.

Adding age points makes it the McIsaac modification: ages 3 to 14 add 1, ages 15 to 44 add 0, and age 45 and up subtract 1.

What the total means:

- 0 to 1: no test and no antibiotics.
- 2 to 3: rapid strep test; treat if positive.
- 4 to 5: test, and treat if positive. The Infectious Diseases Society of America says not to treat on the score alone.

In the room, say each item as you check it.

cards.t: Testing for strep throat (rapid test, culture and antistreptolysin O)
q: how do you test for strep throat
is a negative rapid strep test enough
what does the ASO titer tell you
who should not be tested for strep
cards.x:
Strep is diagnosed with a rapid antigen test and/or a throat culture; the culture is the gold standard. Use the Centor score to decide who gets tested, and don't test children under 3 or patients with obvious viral features.

A negative rapid test in a child or teen should be confirmed with a throat culture. Adults usually don't need the backup culture.

Antistreptolysin O (ASO) titers are not a test for an acute sore throat. They show a past strep infection, and they are used for rheumatic fever. The rapid test or culture is what diagnoses strep throat.

cards.t: Treating strep throat and why we treat it
q: how is strep throat treated
why do we treat strep throat
when can a child go back to school after strep
when does rheumatic fever appear
cards.x:
Treatment is supportive care (fluids, soft diet, rest, pain relief, avoiding irritants) plus penicillin V for 10 days. Amoxicillin can be substituted. A single intramuscular injection of benzathine penicillin G is used if adherence is a worry or the patient can't take pills. With a mild penicillin allergy use cephalexin or cefadroxil; with a severe allergy use clindamycin or a macrolide (azithromycin for 5 days). Don't reach for amoxicillin if mono is still on the table.

We treat to prevent rheumatic fever (treatment works if started within 9 days), to prevent abscess, to help the patient feel better sooner, and to stop spread. Rheumatic fever shows up about 2 to 3 weeks after the infection (range 1 to 5), with a peak at ages 5 to 15. The child can go back to school after 12 to 24 hours of antibiotics.

cards.t: Oral candidiasis (thrush)
q: what is oral thrush
how do you tell thrush from leukoplakia
what does thrush look like
who gets thrush
cards.x:
Oral candidiasis (thrush) is a Candida albicans infection of the mouth, common in infants and in immunosuppressed patients. Patients have a painful mouth, taste changes and painful swallowing. Always ask why it happened: dentures, poor oral hygiene, diabetes, anemia, chemotherapy or radiation, oral or inhaled steroids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, older age, or HIV or other immunosuppression. Trouble or pain swallowing with thrush makes you think of esophageal candidiasis, which is AIDS-defining in HIV.

The look is creamy white, curd-like patches on a red base, usually on the cheek lining and tongue. The key test is that it scrapes off with a tongue depressor, leaving the red base. Leukoplakia and lichen planus don't scrape off. Also look for redness under dentures and cracks at the mouth corners. The diagnosis is clinical, and a potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation shows spores and pseudohyphae. In the exam room, actually scrape it and say what's left.

cards.t: Finding the cause and treating thrush
q: how is oral thrush treated
why do you look for a cause of thrush
how do you prevent thrush from an inhaler
how do you treat thrush in infants
cards.x:
Work up the cause: glucose and A1c for diabetes, an HIV test if there is no clear reason, a blood count, and a medication list. Do a culture if it isn't responding (resistant species).

Treatment begins with saline and peroxide rinses. Mild disease uses nystatin oral suspension (swish) or clotrimazole lozenges for 7 to 14 days. Moderate to severe disease uses oral fluconazole for 7 to 14 days (check drug interactions). Esophageal candidiasis needs systemic fluconazole for 14 to 21 days. Patients with HIV may need a longer course, and refractory cases get itraconazole or voriconazole.

Infants get nystatin to each side of the mouth; if breastfeeding, treat the mother's nipples too, and boil pacifiers and bottle nipples. Then fix the cause: rinse and spit after an inhaled steroid and use a spacer, take dentures out at night and soak them, and control blood sugar.

cards.t: Laryngopharyngeal reflux ("silent reflux")
q: what is laryngopharyngeal reflux
what are the symptoms of silent reflux
why does reflux cause hoarseness
what does the larynx look like in reflux
cards.x:
Laryngopharyngeal reflux is acid reaching the larynx (voice box) and pharynx (throat). It often causes no heartburn at all, so it is called "silent reflux". Patients have morning hoarseness, constant throat clearing, globus (a "lump in my throat"), a chronic cough and a feeling of postnasal drip. Triggers include late or large meals, caffeine, alcohol, chocolate, fatty or spicy food, citrus, tomato, smoking and obesity.

The office exam is often normal, or the back of the throat looks thickened or granular. On laryngoscopy you see redness and swelling of the back of the larynx (the arytenoids), vocal fold swelling and thick mucus. Always feel the neck for nodes.

Two things to tell it from. One is laryngeal carcinoma, the diagnosis the scope exists to exclude (hoarseness past two weeks, more so in a smoker). The other is vocal cord nodules or polyps, which are a discrete lesion rather than diffuse redness.

cards.t: Hoarseness and reflux: when to scope and when to treat
q: when do you refer for laryngoscopy in hoarseness
should you start a proton pump inhibitor for hoarseness
when is endoscopy needed in reflux
cards.x:
Hoarseness that lasts more than 2 weeks is not a diagnosis by itself. Refer for laryngoscopy (a scope exam of the larynx) to rule out cancer and polyps. Clinical guidance is to scope if the voice is not better by 4 weeks. Scope right away if something serious is suspected: a smoker, a neck mass, stridor (noisy breathing) or coughing blood.

Don't start a proton pump inhibitor for hoarseness alone without looking at the larynx. For typical reflux symptoms, an empiric proton pump inhibitor trial (treating without a confirmed diagnosis) is reasonable. Upper endoscopy is for alarm features: trouble or pain swallowing, weight loss, gastrointestinal bleeding or anemia, or persistent vomiting.

In the exam room, ask about morning hoarseness, throat clearing, globus, late meals, smoking and alcohol. Say you would scope anyone whose hoarseness isn't getting better, especially a smoker.

cards.t: Treating reflux and laryngopharyngeal reflux
q: how is laryngopharyngeal reflux treated
when do you take a proton pump inhibitor
what lifestyle changes help reflux
what are the risks of long-term proton pump inhibitors
cards.x:
Reflux treatment starts with lifestyle changes: lose weight, raise the head of the bed, no food 2 to 3 hours before bed, avoid triggers, stop smoking and cut back on alcohol. Add voice care: hydrate, humidify, sip water instead of clearing the throat, and rest the voice.

The medicine is a proton pump inhibitor (such as omeprazole) taken 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast for 8 weeks. Laryngopharyngeal reflux often needs it twice daily for 2 to 3 months, then a taper to the lowest dose that works. Famotidine at bedtime or antacids cover breakthrough symptoms.

If it isn't improving, refer to gastroenterology or an ear, nose and throat specialist. Long-term proton pump inhibitor risks include C. difficile infection, fractures, and low magnesium and vitamin B-12, so use the lowest effective dose.

cards.t: Aphthous ulcers (canker sores)
q: what are aphthous ulcers
what do canker sores look like
what are the types of aphthous ulcers
where do aphthous ulcers occur
cards.x:
Aphthous ulcers are the most common cause of recurrent mouth ulcers in teens and young adults. Patients have painful ulcers, often with burning or tingling before they show up. Triggers include cheek biting or dental work, stress, low iron or zinc, low vitamin B-12 or folate, and certain toothpastes.

The ulcer is round, shallow and painful, with a yellow-gray center and a red halo. They occur mostly on non-keratinized (movable) mucosa: the inside of the cheeks and lips, non-attached gingiva, the underside of the tongue and the soft palate. Three types:

- Minor: under 1 cm, the most common, heals in 7 to 10 days.
- Major: over 1 cm, lasts weeks (often described as more than a month; typically 2 to 6 weeks) and can scar.
- Herpetiform: many 1 to 3 mm ulcers that may merge, each crop usually healing in one to two weeks but recurring in crops (so the problem can last more than a month).

In the exam room, name the location (non-keratinized) and the look (yellow-gray base, red halo).

cards.t: Aphthous ulcers versus herpes simplex, Behçet and cancer
q: how do you tell canker sores from herpes
what systemic disease causes mouth ulcers
when is a mouth ulcer biopsied
what questions do you ask about mouth ulcers
cards.x:
Herpes simplex is different from an aphthous ulcer. It starts with vesicles on keratinized mucosa, and the ulcers cluster rather than sitting alone. There is a prodrome (warning symptoms), and primary infection brings fever and nodes. If herpes is suspected, polymerase chain reaction of the lesion is the most sensitive and specific test.

Behçet syndrome is oral ulcers plus genital ulcers and uveitis (eye inflammation), which is why you ask about genital ulcers and eye symptoms. Also ask about diarrhea and weight loss (Crohn's disease, celiac disease) and HIV.

Frequent, severe or unusual ulcers get a blood count, iron studies, vitamin B-12, folate, zinc, celiac serology and an HIV test. An ulcer that won't heal, especially in a smoker or drinker, needs a biopsy to rule out cancer.

cards.t: Treating aphthous ulcers
q: how are aphthous ulcers treated
do canker sores need treatment
what is used for pain from mouth ulcers
cards.x:
Aphthous ulcers are self-limited, so watching them is fine. Treatment is topical steroids (triamcinolone in dental paste, fluocinonide gel, or dexamethasone swish-and-spit). For pain, use silver nitrate cautery or topical lidocaine (don't swallow it, and be careful in young kids). Other options include antibiotic or antiseptic rinses, dilute water rinses, Lactobacillus capsules and Kanka.

Avoid triggers and correct any deficiency. For severe or frequent disease, use oral steroids or colchicine, and refer (to rheumatology if it is Behçet syndrome).

cards.t: Peritonsillar abscess: the triad
q: what is a peritonsillar abscess
what is the classic triad of peritonsillar abscess
how do you tell peritonsillar abscess from tonsillitis
what does a peritonsillar abscess look like
cards.x:
A peritonsillar abscess is pus between the tonsil capsule and the pharyngeal muscles, a complication of untreated strep or tonsillitis. It is the most common deep neck infection, in teens and young adults, more in males. Patients have a severe sore throat (usually one side), fever, painful swallowing, drooling, a "hot potato" voice, inability to open the jaw, and ear pain on the same side.

The classic triad is trismus (the most reliable sign; the jaw won't open), a uvula deviated away from the abscess, and a muffled voice. The soft palate bulges on one side and the tonsil is pushed toward the midline. Check the airway for stridor and handling of secretions.

Severe tonsillitis is bilateral and symmetric, with no palatal deviation or trismus. A retropharyngeal abscess brings neck stiffness and a widened prevertebral space, in a younger child.

cards.t: Diagnosing and treating peritonsillar abscess
q: how is a peritonsillar abscess treated
how is a peritonsillar abscess confirmed
what are the complications of peritonsillar abscess
when is a tonsillectomy needed
cards.x:
Peritonsillar abscess is a clinical diagnosis, confirmed when pus comes out on drainage. Ultrasound tells abscess from cellulitis and can guide the needle. Computed tomography with contrast is for when the picture is unclear, trismus prevents a look, or you worry it has spread deeper. Also send a blood count, culture of the pus and a Monospot. Bacteria include group A strep, Staphylococcus aureus, H. influenzae and anaerobes such as Fusobacterium.

Secure the airway first. Then needle aspiration or incision and drainage (keep the needle shallow; the carotid artery is behind and lateral). Antibiotics are intravenous amoxicillin-clavulanate or clindamycin, with coverage for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus added if severe; milder cases, or patients who can now swallow, can take amoxicillin-clavulanate or clindamycin by mouth instead. Add pain control and fluids. Tonsillectomy is for recurrent tonsillitis or recurrent abscess, usually after the infection settles.

Complications are airway obstruction and spread to the retropharyngeal space, leading to mediastinitis. In the room, check the airway first, then measure how far the patient can open the mouth.

cards.t: Epiglottitis (supraglottitis)
q: what is epiglottitis
what are the signs of epiglottitis
why not examine the throat in epiglottitis
what is the thumbprint sign
cards.x:
Epiglottitis (also called supraglottitis) is an ear, nose and throat emergency: infection of the epiglottis, the flap that sits above the windpipe. Classically it hits kids 2 to 6 from Hib (H. influenzae type b), a cause that has fallen by over 90 percent since the vaccine. It can also hit adults, and other causes include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus and other strep.

Kids come on suddenly, over hours, with the 4 D's: drooling, dysphagia (trouble swallowing), dysphonia (a "hot potato" muffled voice) and distress. Adults have a severe sore throat, painful swallowing, fever and shortness of breath on a slower course. The patient is irritable, sitting in the tripod or sniffing position, drooling, with a muffled voice; stridor is a late sign.

Do not do a tongue-blade exam, draw blood, or anything else that upsets the patient, because it can trigger complete obstruction. Compare peritonsillar abscess: trismus with uvular deviation, and the mouth can be examined.

cards.t: Diagnosing and managing epiglottitis
q: how is epiglottitis diagnosed
how is epiglottitis treated
what comes first in epiglottitis
how is epiglottitis prevented
cards.x:
Epiglottitis is diagnosed first from the history and how the patient looks. A lateral neck X-ray ("thumbprint sign") is not necessary, and is done only if the patient is stable. Fiberoptic laryngoscopy is the gold standard, done where the airway can be secured. Blood cultures and a swab above the vocal cords come once the airway is safe.

Airway first. Kids go to the operating room for airway control (intubation, with a tracheostomy as backup). Adults get close observation, humidified oxygen, steroids and nebulized epinephrine, with intubation if the airway is closing. Antibiotics are intravenous ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime) plus vancomycin for 7 to 10 days; with a penicillin or cephalosporin allergy use vancomycin plus a quinolone or carbapenem.

Prevention is the Hib vaccine, and rifampin prophylaxis for household contacts when there is an under-vaccinated young child in the home.

cards.t: Infectious mononucleosis (mono) with splenomegaly
q: what is infectious mononucleosis
how does mono present
why is the spleen a concern in mono
how is mono different from strep
cards.x:
Mono is caused by Epstein-Barr virus (90 percent) or cytomegalovirus. It is seen at ages 15 to 24 and spreads through saliva. After a prodrome of malaise, headache and low-grade fever, the triad appears: fever, tonsillar pharyngitis with or without exudate, and cervical lymphadenopathy, often in the posterior nodes. There is heavy fatigue, and a rash after amoxicillin or penicillin.

On exam, look for big tonsils with or without exudate, palatal petechiae, cervical nodes, an enlarged spleen and an enlarged liver. Left upper quadrant or left shoulder pain with low blood pressure means splenic rupture.

Strep has anterior nodes, no splenomegaly and a shorter course. Cytomegalovirus infection looks very similar, but the Monospot is negative.

cards.t: Testing and managing mono
q: why is a Monospot negative early in mono
how is mono diagnosed
when can you return to contact sports after mono
how is mono treated
cards.x:
Mono is tested for with a blood count with differential, which shows lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes, plus a heterophile (Monospot) test. The Monospot is often falsely negative in the first week and in kids under 4, so order Epstein-Barr virus serology (immunoglobulin M means current infection). Also check liver function tests, test for strep if indicated, and use ultrasound to follow the spleen.

Treatment is supportive: fluids, acetaminophen or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and rest. No antiviral works. Steroids are only for when the airway is in trouble. No contact sports or heavy lifting for about 1 month and until the spleen is back to normal. Avoid amoxicillin and ampicillin.

cards.t: Head and neck cancer: red flags in a smoker over 40
k: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
q: when is a neck mass cancer until proven otherwise
what are the red flags for a malignant neck mass
what symptoms suggest head and neck cancer
cards.x:
Unilateral throat pain plus a neck mass in a smoker over 40 is head and neck squamous cell carcinoma until proven otherwise. The malignancy red flags for a neck mass are:

- no infectious source, and present for more than 2 weeks
- larger than 1.5 cm
- firm, non-tender, not mobile
- age over 40
- tobacco and alcohol use

Other symptoms are ear pain with a normal ear exam, hoarseness, trouble or pain swallowing, a non-healing ulcer, bleeding, ill-fitting dentures, trismus (trouble opening the mouth) and weight loss. Human papillomavirus-related oropharynx cancer hits younger non-smokers and can look like a cystic neck mass.

Do a complete head and neck exam. Look at every mucosal surface, palpate the mouth and pharynx, and describe the mass (location, size, mobility, tenderness, consistency). Check the thyroid, other node areas, liver and spleen. Look for leukoplakia and erythroplakia (white and red patches in the mouth). Of erythroplakia, 90 percent are dysplasia or cancer.

cards.t: Working up a suspicious neck mass
q: how do you work up a suspicious neck mass
why not do an excisional biopsy of a neck mass first
how is head and neck cancer treated
cards.x:
The workup is computed tomography of the neck with contrast and a needle biopsy (not an excisional biopsy first). Fiberoptic laryngoscopy looks for the primary tumor. Also human papillomavirus testing, blood counts and a comprehensive metabolic panel; magnetic resonance imaging or positron emission tomography for staging, and a chest X-ray for metastases.

Refer to an ear, nose and throat specialist early. A trial of antibiotics is common, but if the mass is still there, keep working it up. Treatment is surgery with or without radiation or chemotherapy depending on site and stage, plus tobacco and alcohol cessation.

Look-alikes for an ulcer in the mouth: a traumatic ulcer resolves once the denture or sharp tooth is corrected, and a minor aphthous ulcer heals in 7 to 10 days on non-keratinized mucosa (major ones last several weeks).

cards.t: Telling viral pharyngitis, strep and mono apart
q: how do you tell strep from a viral sore throat
how do you tell strep from mono
which sore throat needs a rapid strep test
what is the treatment for each cause of sore throat
cards.x:
Three common sore throats differ in a few reliable ways. In order, they are viral pharyngitis, strep throat, and mononucleosis.

- Typical age: any; 5 to 15; 15 to 24.
- Cough and runny nose: yes; no; usually no.
- Onset: gradual; sudden, with fever; prodrome, then fever.
- Exudate: sometimes, mild; yes, purulent; often, with big tonsils.
- Nodes: mild; tender anterior cervical; posterior and anterior.
- Extra clues: pink eye, hoarseness, vesicles; palatal petechiae, belly pain, scarlet fever rash; heavy fatigue, big spleen, rash with amoxicillin.
- Test: none; rapid strep with or without culture; blood count and Monospot.
- Treatment: supportive; penicillin or amoxicillin for 10 days; supportive, no contact sports.

cards.t: Telling white patches and mouth ulcers apart
q: how do you tell thrush from leukoplakia
what is erythroplakia
what is hairy leukoplakia
what does lichen planus look like in the mouth
cards.x:
A few mouth lesions look alike but mean very different things:

- Thrush: creamy, curd-like plaques that scrape off, leaving a red base. Treat with an antifungal and find the cause.
- Leukoplakia: a white patch that does not scrape off. It is premalignant, and 5 to 20 percent become squamous cell carcinoma, so biopsy.
- Erythroplakia: a red patch that does not scrape off. 90 percent are dysplasia or cancer, so biopsy.
- Hairy leukoplakia: painless, corrugated, on the side of the tongue, and does not scrape off. Do an HIV test.
- Lichen planus: lacy white lines (Wickham striae). Treat symptoms, biopsy if unsure.
- Aphthous ulcer: a shallow ulcer with a yellow-gray base and red halo, on non-keratinized mucosa. A clinical diagnosis, treated with a topical steroid.
- Herpes simplex: vesicles that become clustered ulcers, with a prodrome. Confirm with polymerase chain reaction and treat with acyclovir.

cards.t: The components of a comprehensive history and physical
k: parts of the history and physical
chief complaint history of present illness
q: what are the components of a comprehensive history and physical
in what order do you gather a history and physical
why is the history and physical in a fixed order
cards.x:
A comprehensive history and physical is the full record of an encounter. It is taken in a fixed order so nothing is lost and anyone reading it later finds each piece where they expect it. Here is the order gathered and written:

- Chief complaint: why the patient came, in their own words where possible.
- History of present illness: the narrative of the current problem, built from the seven attributes of a symptom.
- Past medical history: previous illnesses, hospitalizations, surgery.
- Medications and allergies: prescription and over-the-counter, with the reaction for each allergy.
- Family history: heritable disease in first-degree relatives.
- Social history: habits, occupation, exposures, living situation.
- Review of systems: system-by-system screening for symptoms not yet volunteered.
- Physical examination: what you found, described rather than labeled.
- Assessment and plan: differential, working diagnosis, testing, treatment, education, follow-up.

The order is fixed because it supports clinical reasoning. The history narrows the differential before you touch the patient. The examination is then aimed at what the history raised. A history taken out of order tends to produce an examination that wanders.

cards.t: Small groups, simulation and the Objective Structured Clinical Examination
q: what is an Objective Structured Clinical Examination
why do we use small groups and simulation
what does an Objective Structured Clinical Examination test
cards.x:
Small groups, simulation and the OSCE (Objective Structured Clinical Examination) all exist to make you reason out loud, which is the one thing reading cannot teach.

- Small groups: you must justify every request for information, saying what it would tell you about the patient. That turns "order a complete blood count" into a hypothesis with a reason attached.
- Simulation: you reason against a moving target. Vitals are monitored live, laboratory and imaging results arrive during the scenario, and the plan changes as the mannequin changes. A debriefing with reflection and feedback closes each session.
- The OSCE: the whole chain end to end and under time: focused history, focused examination, differentials, studies, diagnosis, treatment plan with patient education, and a one-minute case presentation.

None of them rewards recall alone. The OSCE asks for a plan rather than a list of findings.

cards.t: The oral case presentation
q: how do you give an oral case presentation
what is the purpose of an oral presentation
what are pertinent positives and negatives
cards.x:
An oral case presentation is a well-organized vignette that describes the patient and the clinical problem, not the written note read aloud. The goal is to help listeners visualize the patient and understand the problem.

- Opening statement: include the past medical history and the chief complaint.
- Content: pertinent positives and negatives, from both the history and the physical examination.
- Order: mostly the order in which you obtained the history and performed the examination.
- Delivery: try not to read your notes.
