The test of a good presentation is that it leads your listener to the same differential you formulated. Choosing what counts as pertinent is the clinical reasoning being shown; a presentation that includes everything has made no decisions.

cards.t: Comprehensive versus focused history and physical
k: one system up one system down
q: what is the difference between a comprehensive and a focused history and physical
how far does a focused exam reach
does a focused encounter need a full plan
cards.x:
A focused encounter narrows both the history and the examination. It is not a comprehensive encounter written up more briefly. It is not a full history with a short exam either. In a comprehensive encounter all of these are full: the history of present illness, review of systems, past medical, social and family history, and medications and allergies. The exam is head to toe. In a focused encounter each is narrowed, and the exam covers the systems pertinent to the complaint.

Narrowing the data does not narrow what you are expected to conclude. A focused encounter still produces differentials, laboratory and imaging studies, a diagnosis, and a treatment plan including patient education.

How far should a focused exam reach? Examine the systems pertinent to the chief complaint and the positive history. When in doubt, go one system up and one system down. Two questions settle the rest. What must be examined to rule out the worst-case scenario? What are your differentials, and how do you rule each in or out?

cards.t: The complete history and physical versus the SOAP note
q: what is the difference between a history and physical and a SOAP note
what goes in the subjective and objective sections
when do you use a SOAP note
cards.x:
Both document an encounter, but they differ in scope and purpose. The complete history and physical is comprehensive: the entire history and a head-to-toe exam, used for a new patient, an admission or an annual comprehensive visit. A SOAP (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) note is problem-focused: used for a visit addressing a defined problem, and for follow-up, and its exam is focused but always includes a general assessment or impression.

The four parts of the note are:

- Subjective: what the patient said (narrative history, pertinent positives and negatives, medical and surgical history, family and social history, review of systems, medications, allergies).
- Objective: what you found (observations, measurements and tests, the focused exam, always a general assessment or impression).
- Assessment: what you concluded (the diagnosis drawn from history, exam and testing, plus chronic and concurrent conditions).
- Plan: what you will do (disposition, testing, treatment, referrals, patient education, follow-up).

cards.t: Rules for documenting a history and physical
k: how to write up a history and physical
subjective versus objective in a note
q: what are the rules for documenting a history and physical
why describe findings instead of writing normal
what if you did not do part of the exam
why keep subjective and objective separate
cards.x:
Several documentation rules matter most:

- Describe findings rather than writing normal, abnormal or unremarkable. A description communicates what you actually observed. A label communicates only that you formed an opinion.
- Use no abbreviations, with no allowance for "defined on first use".
- Keep subjective and objective information in their own sections. Blending them is one of the commonest documentation errors. It hides which claims are the patient's and which are yours.
- If you did not do something, document why. You may not invent a finding. This is the one rule treated as absolute.
- You may not write your note with another student, even when you saw the same patient.
- Review the grading rubric and comments on prior assignments before submitting. Prior feedback is the most direct guide to what still needs fixing.
- Reusing your own earlier work counts as plagiarism. Work submitted for credit must be original, and work is not original when it has been submitted before. So even reusing your own template from an earlier assignment is the trap.

cards.t: Involving the patient in healthcare communication
k: talking to the patient not the interpreter
q: who do you look at when someone else answers for the patient
why must communication adapt to each patient
how should you respond to feedback
cards.x:
Communication is a graded skill, and it should adapt in style and content for each patient rather than follow one fixed script.

The rule stated most emphatically is this. When someone other than the patient is supplying the answers, always look at and interact with the patient, not with whoever is speaking. The encounter is with the patient even when the words come from elsewhere. In the Objective Structured Clinical Examination the "patient" gives no verbal responses beyond identifying data, and the facilitator answers for them. That is exactly the situation this rule is built for.

A related expectation is to accept constructive feedback and modify your behavior. Expect different facilitators to give different feedback. That variation is anticipated rather than a contradiction to be resolved.

cards.t: The skin: functions and layers
q: what are the functions of the skin
what are the layers of the skin
why does depth matter for lesion names
cards.x:
The skin has five functions: protection of internal structures, prevention of entry of germs, temperature regulation, excretion and production of vitamin D.

It has three layers, and depth is why some lesion names differ. A lesion confined to the epidermis is superficial. That is an erosion, which stays moist and does not bleed. If it reaches the dermis, where the vessels run, it can bleed and scar. That is an ulcer. A nodule sits deeper in the dermis than a papule, and a cyst may sit deeper still, in the subcutaneous layer.

cards.t: Skin glands and hair types
q: what do eccrine, apocrine and sebaceous glands do
what is the difference between vellus and terminal hair
which glands become active at puberty
cards.x:
Three types of gland:

- Sudoriferous (eccrine) glands make sweat, which maintains body temperature.
- Apocrine glands make pheromones and become active during puberty.
- Sebaceous glands make sebum, surround the hair follicle, and keep hair and skin moist.

Two types of hair: vellus hair is short and fine and covers the body. Terminal hair is coarse and grows on the scalp and in the pubic, axillary and beard areas.

cards.t: The five features used to describe any skin lesion
q: how do you describe a skin lesion
what are the features of a skin lesion description
why is descriptive vocabulary important
cards.x:
Five features describe any lesion: distribution (location), configuration (the shape lesions make together), morphology (form and structure), color and texture. This vocabulary is the backbone of how you write notes and communicate with other providers. It carries over to the exam of every other organ system, not just the skin.

Of the five, distribution is often the fastest route to a diagnosis (see the distribution patterns). The shape terms (configuration) and the lesion names (morphology) give the rest of the description.

cards.t: Distribution patterns and what they suggest
q: what does lesion distribution tell you
where does psoriasis appear
which rash follows a dermatome
what does sun-exposed distribution suggest
cards.x:
Distribution is often the fastest route to a diagnosis. Terms include unilateral, bilateral, symmetric, asymmetric, photodistribution, intertriginous, flexural, extensor, palmar-plantar and hair-bearing areas. Classic pairings:

- Generalized or diffuse: allergic reactions.
- Regional (confined to one body area): tinea capitis.
- Sun-exposed (photodistribution): skin cancers.
- Dermatome: herpes zoster.
- Extensor: psoriasis (the elbows and knees are the classic extensor sites).
- Flexor: atopic dermatitis is the classic example (the inner elbows and the backs of the knees); intertrigo, inflammation in skin folds, is also paired with this pattern.
- Intertriginous (creases and folds): involvement of skin folds.

cards.t: Lesion configuration terms (annular, grouped, linear and more)
q: what does annular mean
what does configuration mean for skin lesions
what is the difference between confluent and discrete
cards.x:
Configuration is the shape the lesions make together:

- Annular: ring-shaped, round.
- Arciform: forms arcs or curves.
- Confluent: lesions run together. Discrete: lesions remain separate.
- Grouped: a cluster of lesions.
- Gyrate: twisted, coiled, spiral, snakelike. Serpiginous: snake-like.
- Iris (target): shaped like a bull's eye.
- Linear: forms a line or stripe.
- Reticular: lacy or networked pattern.

Two more terms, herpetiform and zosteriform, are named for infections and are easy to swap (they are explained on their own).

cards.t: Herpetiform versus zosteriform
q: what is the difference between herpetiform and zosteriform
what does herpetiform mean
what does zosteriform mean
cards.x:
Both terms are named for an infection, which is what makes them easy to swap.

- Herpetiform: grouped papules or vesicles arranged as in herpes simplex, a cluster.
- Zosteriform: clustered in a dermatomal distribution, as in herpes zoster, a band that follows one nerve's territory.

So the question to ask is whether the lesions are just a cluster (herpetiform) or a cluster that follows a dermatome (zosteriform).

cards.t: Primary skin lesions and the one-centimeter hinge
q: what is a primary skin lesion
what is the size cutoff between macule and patch
what is the difference between a vesicle and a bulla
how do you remember the primary lesion pairs
cards.x:
A primary lesion forms first and results directly from the disease. Identifying it is the key to interpreting and describing the rash, because every later description depends on getting it right.

One centimeter is the hinge. Three matched pairs turn on it: flat discoloration (macule under one centimeter, patch over), solid elevated lesion (papule under, plaque over), and fluid-filled elevation (vesicle under, bulla over). Learn the three pairs and you have six of the terms. That is why a ruler is on the equipment list.

Different courses use different cutoffs: for the macule and patch line this physical diagnosis course uses one centimeter, while another course teaches five millimeters for the same lesions. Neither is wrong, and each course examines its own convention, so use the number that belongs to the course you are being tested in.

cards.t: Macule versus patch
q: what is a macule
what is the difference between a macule and a patch
what are examples of a patch
cards.x:
A macule is a circumscribed (well-bordered), flat discoloration, brown, blue, red or hypopigmented, under one centimeter. A freckle is the example. Run a finger across it and you feel nothing, which is what makes it a macule rather than a papule.

A patch is the same flat discoloration but larger than one centimeter. It can be a large macule, or several macules that have coalesced (run together). Examples are vitiligo and café au lait spots.

cards.t: Solid raised lesions: papule, plaque, nodule and tumor
q: what is the difference between a papule and a plaque
what is a nodule
when is a skin lesion called a tumor
what is the difference between a nodule and a papule
cards.x:
All four are palpable, elevated, solid lesions; elevation is the whole distinction from a macule, and it is found by touch rather than by looking.

- Papule: under one centimeter (nevi, warts, lichen planus).
- Plaque: over one centimeter, plateau-like (elevated, flat-topped, firm and rough), occupying a large area compared with its elevation; may be coalesced papules. Psoriasis is the example.
- Nodule: elevated, firm, circumscribed, round or ellipsoid, and deeper in the dermis than a papule; 1 to 2 centimeters (one textbook says larger than 0.5 centimeter). Basal cell carcinoma and neurofibromatosis are examples.
- Tumor: over 2 centimeters (neoplasms).

So a lesion at 18 millimeters is a nodule, and over 20 millimeters it would be a tumor.

cards.t: Vesicle, bulla and pustule
q: what is the difference between a vesicle and a bulla
what is a pustule
how do you tell a vesicle from a pustule
cards.x:
These are superficial elevations of the skin filled with something:

- Vesicle: filled with fluid, under one centimeter. A blister; herpes simplex is the classic example.
- Bulla: the same fluid-filled elevation but over one centimeter. A large blister. Size is the only thing separating the two terms.
- Pustule: filled with purulent (pus) material, usually under one centimeter. Acne and impetigo are examples. Contents, not size, separate a pustule from a vesicle.

Vesicles clustered as in herpes are described as herpetiform.

cards.t: Wheal and cyst: lesions defined by something other than size
q: what is a wheal
what is a cyst
how is a cyst different from a nodule
why is a wheal gone at the next visit
cards.x:
Two primary lesions are defined by something other than size.

A wheal is an elevated, irregularly shaped area of cutaneous edema (swelling of the skin), solid and variable in size. It is the only transient primary lesion, as in an allergic reaction. If it is gone by the next visit, that is the finding, not a missed examination.

A cyst is elevated, circumscribed and encapsulated (it has a capsule), in the dermis or subcutaneous layer, with liquid or semisolid contents; a sebaceous cyst is the example. The capsule is what separates it from a nodule you can feel at the same depth.

cards.t: Secondary skin lesions: crust, scale, fissure and excoriation
q: what is a secondary skin lesion
what is the difference between crust and scale
what is an excoriation
what causes secondary lesions
cards.x:
A secondary lesion is a change in a primary lesion over time, from disease progression, from treatment, or from manipulation such as picking or scratching. The patient's own hands can change the examination.

- Crust: a collection of cellular debris, dried serum and blood, a scab. The earlier primary lesion is usually a vesicle, bulla or pustule.
- Scale: a thin flake of exfoliated (shed) epidermis, as in dandruff or cradle cap. Scale is shed skin; crust is dried serum, blood and debris.
- Fissure: a linear crack in the skin, as in athlete's foot.
- Excoriation: an abrasion or scratch mark, linear or rounded, as in a scratched insect bite. It tells you the eruption itches.

cards.t: Erosion versus ulcer
q: what is the difference between an erosion and an ulcer
why does an erosion not bleed
which skin lesion scars
cards.x:
Depth decides everything. An erosion is loss of the superficial epidermis only, with no involvement of the dermis. The surface is moist but does not bleed, because the dermis has not been breached. An example is the moist area left after a bulla or vesicle ruptures.

An ulcer is deeper loss of the epidermis and/or dermis. It may bleed and it may scar, as in the stasis ulcer of venous insufficiency. So an erosion stops at the epidermis, is moist, and does not bleed or scar; an ulcer reaches the dermis, may bleed, and may scar.

cards.t: Scar versus keloid
q: what is the difference between a scar and a keloid
what are hypertrophic and atrophic scars
who gets keloids
cards.x:
A scar (cicatrix) is the replacement of destroyed tissue by fibrous tissue. It may be thick and pink (hypertrophic) or thin and white (atrophic), and it does not extend beyond the injured area.

A keloid is a scar that grows beyond the wound. That last point is what separates the two. A keloid is a firm, raised scar-tissue lesion, more common in darker-skinned individuals. It is commonest on the shoulders and upper chest but also arises at piercing sites, including the ear.

cards.t: Lichenification
q: what is lichenification
what causes lichenification
what does lichenification look like
cards.x:
Lichenification is thickening of the skin with accentuation of the skin lines: the epidermis is roughened and thickened. It is caused by chronic irritation, and atopic dermatitis is the example. The exaggerated creases are the finding.

In the atopic dermatitis example the distribution is flexural, and the scratch marks (excoriations) alongside it explain the mechanism: the skin thickens in response to the chronic irritation.

cards.t: Collarette scale
k: fine scale attached at the periphery
q: what is collarette scale
where is collarette scale seen
cards.x: Collarette scale is a fine scale on the edge of an inflammatory lesion, attached at the periphery and detached in the center. Which end is attached is the entire definition. It is seen in pityriasis rosea.

cards.t: Warts, corns and calluses
q: what is a wart
what is the difference between a corn and a callus
what causes warts
cards.x:
Three common skin growths:

- Verrucae (warts) are caused by human papillomavirus. They are small harmless tumors of the skin, gray to flesh-colored nodules raised from the surface, sometimes with rough hornlike projections.
- A corn is smaller than a callus, usually over a non-weight-bearing area of the foot, and has a conical structure of keratin pointing toward the dermis.
- A callus is a thickening of epidermal keratin, usually on the sole of the foot, at the ball or heel.

cards.t: The dermatological history: the five questions and bugs, drugs, contact
q: what do you ask in a dermatological history
what does bugs drugs contact mean
what are the core questions for a rash
cards.x:
Ask five core questions. Where did the problem first appear? What did it look like? How has it progressed or changed? Are there any associated symptoms? What treatment has been tried?

"Bugs, drugs, contact" is the fastest way to remember what else to ask. Bugs: family members or contacts with the same problem, and travel. Drugs: systemic medications, both over-the-counter and prescription. Contact: allergens and irritants from hobbies, occupation and environment.

Also ask about onset (duration, acute versus chronic) and relationships (season, travel, heat or cold, previous reactions, drugs, menses). Ask about skin symptoms (itch, pain, tingling), past medical and family history, and psychosocial factors.

cards.t: Details to ask about in a skin history
q: what do you ask about an existing skin lesion
what family history matters in dermatology
can stress cause skin disease
cards.x:
For an existing skin abnormality, ask about changes in color, shape (border, elevation, diameter) and size, pain, easy bleeding, and non-healing areas.

Family history asks about skin cancer, psoriasis, allergies, infestations and infections. Psychosocial history covers personal habits and exposures. Psychological stress is seldom the sole cause, but it can make many skin diseases (dermatoses) worse.

cards.t: Pruritus (itching)
q: what is pruritus
what causes generalized itching without a rash
is pruritus a diagnosis
what sensations should you ask about
cards.x:
Pruritus is the sensation that causes the desire to scratch. It is not a diagnosis, and treating it as one is an error. Generalized itching with no obvious reason has a wide differential: dry skin, aging, pregnancy, uremia, jaundice, lymphomas, leukemias, drug reaction and lice.

Other sensations to ask about are burning, pain or tenderness, tingling, and a creeping or crawling feeling, and whether it is intermittent or continuous.

cards.t: Poor hygiene as a finding
q: what does poor skin hygiene suggest
what do you do when a patient's hygiene is inadequate
cards.x: Patients with cognitive problems may not attend to hygiene. If the hygiene of the skin, hair or nails appears inadequate, that is itself a finding. Follow up by assessing the social history, cognition, and the ability to perform activities of daily living.

cards.t: Diascopy: does the lesion blanch?
q: what is diascopy
how do you tell hemorrhage from vascular engorgement
what does non-blanching mean
cards.x:
Diascopy is the one maneuver that sorts vascular lesions. Press a piece of clear glass or plastic against the skin and look at the lesion under pressure. If the color fades (blanches), there is vascular engorgement. If it does not fade, the cause is hemorrhage in the skin.

If the spots persist under the glass, with no blanching, it is blood that has leaked out of the vessels. If the color had faded, it would be engorged vessels instead. One maneuver separates blanching lesions (engorged vessels) from non-blanching ones (blood leaked out of the vessels).

cards.t: Petechiae, purpura and ecchymosis
q: what is the difference between petechiae and purpura
what size is an ecchymosis
do petechiae blanch
cards.x:
These are the same finding at three sizes, and none of them blanches, because the blood is outside the vessels.

- Petechiae: reddish-purple macules under 3 millimeters.
- Purpura: reddish-purple macules 3 millimeters to 1 centimeter.
- Ecchymosis: purple or purplish-blue macules over 1 centimeter. Ecchymoses also fade over time as the leaked blood breaks down.

cards.t: Cherry angioma, telangiectasia and spider angioma
q: what is a cherry angioma
what is the difference between a spider angioma and telangiectasia
which vascular lesions blanch
cards.x:
Three vascular lesions that, unlike the non-blanching bleeding spots, are made of vessels:

- Cherry angioma (Campbell De Morgan spots): dome shaped, bright red to violet or black. It sometimes blanches, so it sits awkwardly between the groups and is best learned by its shape.
- Telangiectasia: fine, irregular blood vessels. It blanches.
- Spider angioma: a central red macule with radiating spider-like arms. It blanches.

cards.t: Dermatographism and the triple response of Lewis
q: what is dermatographism
what is the triple response of Lewis
what are the stages of the triple response
cards.x:
Dermatographism means "writing on skin". It is a hive-type (urticarial) reaction. It is often called allergic, but it is really an exaggerated skin response to pressure, not a true allergy. Firm stroking of the skin produces the triple response of Lewis, in three steps:

1. An initial red line, from capillary dilatation.
2. A reflex flare with broadening erythema (redness), from arteriolar dilatation.
3. Formation of a linear wheal, from transudation of fluid (edema).

cards.t: Pressure (decubitus) ulcer stages I to IV
q: what are the stages of a pressure ulcer
what is a stage I pressure ulcer
what separates stage III from stage IV
cards.x:
Pressure ulcers are staged by depth.

- Stage I: intact skin with erythema that fails to blanch with pressure, plus a change in temperature (warmth or coolness), consistency (firm or boggy), sensation (pain or itching) and color.
- Stage II: partial thickness skin loss involving the epidermis, the dermis or both.
- Stage III: full thickness skin loss with necrosis of subcutaneous tissue; it may extend to, but not through, the underlying fascia (the tough sheet over the muscle).
- Stage IV: full thickness skin loss with destruction of tissue, muscle and/or bone.

The stage I and II line is whether the skin is broken. The stage III and IV line is whether the damage goes deeper than the fat: once muscle, bone or supporting structures are involved, it is stage IV.

cards.t: Tinea (ringworm) infections by body site
q: what is tinea
what does tinea corporis look like
what does tinea capitis look like
what do the tinea names mean
cards.x:
Tinea infections are named by site: corporis (body), pedis (foot), barbae (beard), cruris (groin), capitis (scalp) and unguium (nails).

- Tinea pedis: dry, scaling, or macerated (soggy) fissuring of the spaces between the toes.
- Tinea corporis: scaling, sharply demarcated round plaques with central clearing. The active advancing edge with a quiet middle earns it the name ringworm, and its configuration term is annular.
- Tinea capitis: round scaling patches of hair loss (alopecia) with hairs broken off close to the scalp.

cards.t: Basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma of the skin
q: what does basal cell carcinoma look like
what does squamous cell carcinoma look like
how do you tell basal cell from squamous cell carcinoma
cards.x:
Basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma are two skin cancers you tell apart by the surface.

- Basal cell carcinoma: found on the face. It is a translucent, pearly nodule with a depressed center and raised borders, and it may ulcerate. A non-healing ulcer is the other presentation. A raised, shiny, slow-growing lesion with visible telangiectasia (tiny visible blood vessels) on the ear should raise the same suspicion.
- Squamous cell carcinoma: found on the face and other sun-exposed areas. It is a red, scaling, crusting nodule or plaque that can ulcerate and bleed.

Compare the surface: scaling and crusted in squamous cell carcinoma, translucent and pearly in basal cell carcinoma.

cards.t: Malignant melanoma and its warning letters (A to F)
q: what are the ABCDE warning signs of melanoma
what does melanoma look like
what diameter is suspicious for melanoma
what is the F in the melanoma list
cards.x:
Malignant melanoma is a skin cancer to look for in changing nevi (moles). It looks like an irregularly colored plaque with sharp notches and variation of pigment. The warning signs are the letters (the full list runs on to G, growing):

- A: asymmetry or shape.
- B: border irregularity.
- C: color variation.
- D: diameter larger than 6 millimeters, about the width of a pencil eraser.
- E: evolving, elevation.
- F: family history.

An advanced melanoma can show every letter at once: asymmetric, a notched irregular border, marked variation in pigment, and well beyond 6 millimeters; early ones may show only one or two.

cards.t: Kaposi's sarcoma
q: what is Kaposi's sarcoma
what does Kaposi's sarcoma look like
what is the most common neoplasm in AIDS
cards.x: Kaposi's sarcoma is a skin cancer whose lesions can be widely spread over the legs, trunk, arms, neck and head. Lesions start light-colored and coalesce into darker ones: dark blue-purple macules, papules, nodules and plaques. It is the most frequent neoplasm (new growth) in patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome.

cards.t: Types of alopecia and other hair findings
q: what is trichotillomania
what is hirsutism
what are the types of alopecia
what are nits
cards.x:
Alopecia is diffuse, patchy or total hair loss. Note the distribution on inspection, because that is what separates the causes.

- Androgenic alopecia: male pattern baldness.
- Alopecia areata: a chronic inflammatory disease of the hair follicles, associated with autoimmune disorders; hair loss in multiple round patches with "exclamation point" hairs.
- Trichotillomania: an urge to pull out hair, producing bald patches, single or multiple, from a few square centimeters to the entire scalp.

Hirsutism is increased hair growth in women, in a male pattern of distribution. Lice show as tiny white ovoid granules (nits) stuck to hairs; a magnifying glass aids inspection.

cards.t: Telling patchy hair loss apart: tinea capitis, alopecia areata, trichotillomania
q: how do you tell alopecia areata from tinea capitis
what are exclamation point hairs
how is trichotillomania different from alopecia areata
cards.x:
Three causes of patchy hair loss are told apart by what is left behind.

- Tinea capitis: scaling patches, with hairs broken off close to the scalp.
- Alopecia areata: smooth patches with no scale, with "exclamation point" hairs (a few follicles still trying), best seen at the margins as tapered hairs. Seeing them should trigger alopecia areata.
- Trichotillomania: patches from pulling, with neither scale nor exclamation point hairs.

cards.t: Koilonychia, onycholysis and nail pitting
q: what is koilonychia
what causes onycholysis
what is nail pitting
cards.x:
Three nail findings, each with its own cause or association:

- Koilonychia: spoon-shaped, concave nails; the nail plate thins and becomes inverted.
- Onycholysis: painless separation of the nail plate from the nail bed, starting distally, with several or all nails usually affected. Causes include local irritation (chemical exposure, prolonged immersion in water), fungal infection, psoriasis, medications such as tetracycline, and trauma.
- Nail pitting: dystrophy (abnormal growth) of the nail plate with areas of small depressions or "pits". Psoriasis can cause both pitting and onycholysis.

cards.t: Beau's lines and Mee's lines
q: what are Beau's lines
how do Beau's lines date an illness
what is the difference between Beau's and Mee's lines
cards.x:
Both are transverse (across the nail) changes. Beau's lines are transverse depressions you can feel. Mee's lines are transverse lines of color.

Beau's lines work like a clock. The nail grows out at a roughly known rate. So a transverse depression halfway up the nail dates the insult to an illness about 3 months before the visit. That sends you back to the history with a specific date in mind.

cards.t: Nail clubbing and paronychia
q: what is clubbing
what is paronychia
how do you measure clubbing
cards.x:
Clubbing: the angle between the nail base and the finger is greater than 180 degrees, and the end of the finger becomes rounded and bulbous. Sight the finger from the side; the angle is the measurable part rather than the impression of bulbousness.

Paronychia is a soft tissue infection around the nail, at the cuticle or nail fold. Acute paronychia is painful and purulent; it also occurs in a chronic form.

cards.t: Nail color and bleeding findings
q: what does a green nail mean
what are splinter hemorrhages
what are Terry's nails
what does a brown-black nail suggest
cards.x:
Nail inspection covers shape, size, color, brittleness, hemorrhages, lines and grooves, clubbing, and pitting. Color and bleeding clues:

- Green nail: Pseudomonas infection.
- Brown-black nail: think melanoma.
- Terry's nails: the proximal portion is white and the distal portion dark.
- Subungual hematoma: hemorrhage to the nail plate.
- Splinter hemorrhages: hemorrhage of the distal capillary loop.

cards.t: Setting up the skin examination
q: how do you set up a skin exam
what equipment do you need for a skin exam
why is lighting important in a skin exam
what are the four principles of physical examination
cards.x:
The four principles of examination are inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation. That order holds for every body system except the abdominal examination, and some systems do not use all four.

For the skin exam, the equipment is a ruler, a light source, a magnifying lens, and gloves for any open lesions. The patient is in a gown. That way you can inspect hair, front and back body surfaces, palms and soles, nails and the spaces between fingers and toes. Inspect the entire skin surface in good light, preferably natural light or artificial light that resembles it. Artificial light may distort skin tone.

cards.t: The six features assessed in a skin exam
q: what are the six things assessed in a skin exam
how do you check skin temperature
what does rubor mean
cards.x:
Six features are assessed by inspection, palpation, or both. Color and lesions begin with inspection and the rest need touch.

- Color: increase or decrease in pigmentation, erythema/rubor (redness; the two terms are interchangeable), pallor, jaundice, cyanosis.
- Moisture: dryness, sweating, oiliness.
- Temperature: warmth or coolness. Use the dorsal (back) aspect of the hands.
- Texture: roughness or smoothness.
- Mobility and turgor.
- Lesions: distribution, configuration, morphology, color, texture.

cards.t: Skin mobility and turgor
q: what is skin turgor
what does reduced skin mobility suggest
what does slow skin recoil mean
cards.x:
Mobility and turgor are two separate checks, and they point in different directions.

- Mobility: the skin lifts up with ease. Reduced mobility suggests edema.
- Turgor: the skin quickly resumes its shape. If the skin remains elevated (it is slow to snap back), think dehydration. Keep them straight: edema reduces mobility, while dehydration reduces turgor.

cards.t: Central versus peripheral cyanosis
q: what is the difference between central and peripheral cyanosis
what causes central cyanosis
what causes peripheral cyanosis
cards.x: Central versus peripheral cyanosis (bluish color) is a two-organ distinction. Central cyanosis is often due to inadequate oxygenation in the lungs; peripheral cyanosis is usually due to inadequate circulation. Same color, different organ: when skin is blue, ask whether the problem is oxygenation in the lungs or circulation.

cards.t: Examining the hair and scalp
q: how do you examine the scalp
what should a normal scalp look like
what do you inspect in the hair
cards.x: Inspect the hair for color, distribution and quantity, and palpate it for texture. Separate the hair into sections to observe the scalp, and inspect behind the ears and the occiput (the back of the head). A normal scalp is clean, with no lesions, discolorations, flaking or parasites.

cards.t: The eye history: four axes and what the answers suggest
q: how do you take an eye history
what do flashes and floaters mean
what does bilateral vision loss suggest
what does itching with tearing suggest
cards.x:
Assess any eye complaint on four axes: time course, precipitating factors, palliative or exacerbating variables (what helps or worsens it), and vision loss or visual deficits. Then some answers point to a cause:

- Bilateral visual loss, especially sudden: a neurologic cause is likely rather than an eye one; gradual loss in both eyes is often cataract or similar eye disease.
- Multiple new flashes or floaters: retinal tear or vitreous hemorrhage. A single floater is probably benign.
- Rapid deterioration: vascular causes. Gradual loss: cataract and the like.
- Itching plus excessive tearing: allergic.
- Deep pain: acute narrow angle glaucoma.

cards.t: Does a topical anesthetic relieve the eye pain?
q: what does it mean if eye pain is relieved by anesthetic drops
how do you tell surface from deep eye pain
why does a corneal injury feel better with numbing drops
cards.x: A topical anesthetic can help sort the cause of eye pain. If the pain is relieved by the topical anesthetic, it suggests a surface problem, such as a corneal injury, which feels better. If the pain is not relieved, it may come from a deeper source.

cards.t: Other questions in the eye history
q: what else do you ask in an eye history
why ask about acid or alkali in an eye splash
which systemic diseases matter for the eye
cards.x:
Beyond the four axes, the eye history also covers corrective lenses; acute or chronic eye problems such as glaucoma; eye medications such as antiglaucoma drops or topical antibiotics; and eye surgery history. In eye trauma, tetanus status matters, and after a chemical splash you must establish whether the fluid was an acid or an alkali.

Three systemic diseases deserve a specific question: diabetes, hypertension and human immunodeficiency virus, the last because it will affect basically any cause of eye disease.

cards.t: Chemosis and hyperemia
q: what is chemosis
what is hyperemia of the eye
what is the difference between chemosis and hyperemia
cards.x: Two eye terms that sound alike mean different things. Chemosis is swelling and inflammation of the conjunctiva itself, not of the lids or the globe. Hyperemia is injection of the superficially visible vessels of the conjunctiva, episclera or sclera, the visible redness.

cards.t: Acute versus gradual, painful versus painless vision loss
q: what causes acute painless vision loss
what causes acute painful vision loss
what causes gradual painless vision loss
what causes painful vision loss in both eyes
cards.x:
Sorting by time course, side and pain narrows the cause:

- Acute, one eye, painless: retinal vascular occlusion, retinal detachment, vitreous hemorrhage or macular degeneration.
- Acute, one eye, painful: usually the cornea and anterior chamber. Think corneal abrasion or ulcer, uveitis, traumatic hyphema, or acute narrow angle glaucoma.
- Acute, both eyes, painful: thermal, radiation or chemical exposure.
- Gradual, painless: simple glaucoma or cataract.

cards.t: What the quality of eye pain points to
k: pain on eye movement optic neuritis
q: what does eye pain with blinking suggest
what does eye pain on movement suggest
what does photophobia with eye pain mean
what does eye pain with headache mean
cards.x:
Eye pain, qualified, points to a cause:

- Pain with blinking: corneal abrasion or foreign body.
- Gritty: conjunctivitis.
- With photophobia (light sensitivity): iris inflammation.
- With headache: acute narrow angle glaucoma.
- On eye motion: optic neuritis.
- With temporal pain: temporal arteritis.

cards.t: Eye discharge, tearing and dryness
q: what does purulent eye discharge mean
what does watery discharge from the eye suggest
what causes excessive tearing or dry eyes
cards.x:
The type of discharge sorts the cause. Purulent discharge suggests a bacterial infection, while watery or mucoid discharge suggests allergy or a virus.

Excessive tearing can come from obstruction in the lacrimal apparatus (the tear-drainage system), and dryness from Sjogren's syndrome.

cards.t: Double vision and the cranial nerves
q: which cranial nerves cause double vision
what does horizontal diplopia mean
what does vertical diplopia mean
how do you remember diplopia nerves
cards.x:
Double vision follows a pattern:

- Horizontal diplopia (images side by side): a palsy of cranial nerve III or VI.
- Vertical diplopia (images on top of each other): a palsy of cranial nerve III or IV.

The shortcut is "three for both of those". The third nerve can cause either pattern. The sixth nerve alone can cause the side-by-side kind. The fourth nerve alone can cause the on-top-of-each-other kind.

Diplopia otherwise means faulty alignment or a neurological problem: brainstem or cerebellar lesions, or weakness of one or more extraocular muscles. Look for a compensatory head posture.

cards.t: The order of the eye examination
k: visual acuity vital sign of the eye
q: what is the order of the eye examination
why check pupils before dilating
why is visual acuity called the vital sign of the eye
can you palpate the globe in trauma
cards.x:
The order is: inspection, external examination, cornea without light, lens and pupils, visual acuity (the vital sign of the eye), visual fields, ocular motility, pupillary reactions. Then come corneal reflection, special tests, slit lamp, ocular pressure, and finally direct ophthalmoscopy.

Pupillary reactions are checked before dilating. In trauma, do not palpate the globe.

cards.t: Common mistakes in the eye examination
q: what are common mistakes in the eye exam
why is orbital cellulitis dangerous
why avoid a topical steroid in an infectious red eye
when should floaters make you think of detachment
cards.x: The common mistakes are: failing to look in both eyes, to examine the cornea and lens, to test acuity adequately, to identify a field defect, or to evaluate all fundal structures; failing to recognize a ruptured globe (or putting too much pressure on one); failing to treat multiple floaters or new flashes as a possible detachment; failing to document adequately; failing to recognize an infectious red eye before prescribing a topical steroid; and failing to differentiate preseptal from orbital cellulitis, because the latter can lead to death.

cards.t: Eyebrow, eyelid and sclera findings and what they suggest
q: what does xanthelasma suggest
what is the difference between entropion and ectropion
what causes blue sclera
what do sparse lateral eyebrows suggest
cards.x:
External findings carry clues:

- Scaly eyebrows: seborrheic dermatitis.
- Lateral sparseness of the eyebrows: hypothyroidism.
- Xanthelasma: raised yellowish plaques along the nasal portions of the lids; consider lipid disorders.
- Ectropion: the lid turns out. Entropion: the lid turns in. Trichiasis: lashes misdirected posteriorly (toward the eye).
- Yellow sclera: liver disease. Blue sclera: osteogenesis imperfecta.

cards.t: Ptosis (drooping eyelid)
q: what causes ptosis
what is senile ptosis
what diseases cause a drooping eyelid
cards.x: Ptosis is a drooping upper eyelid. Causes include myasthenia gravis, oculomotor nerve damage and sympathetic damage (Horner syndrome). Senile ptosis comes from weakened muscle, relaxed tissue and the weight of herniated fat. It may also be congenital.

cards.t: Hordeolum versus chalazion
q: what is the difference between a hordeolum and a chalazion
which lid lump is painful
where does a chalazion point
cards.x: A hordeolum (stye) is a painful infection at the lid's edge. A chalazion is chronic, non-painful and involves the meibomian glands; it is generally not at the lid margin and points inside the lid. The quick contrasts are painful infection at the edge versus painless chronic lump pointing inward.

cards.t: Examining for proptosis (bulging eyes)
q: how do you check for proptosis
what causes proptosis
how do you recognize exophthalmos
cards.x:
To check for proptosis (a bulging eye), stand behind the seated patient and look down from above. Draw the lid slightly upward to compare the corneas against the lower lids.

Causes are retrobulbar hemorrhage (bleeding behind the eye), orbital cellulitis, an orbital tumor and Graves disease.

cards.t: Testing for nasolacrimal duct obstruction
q: how do you test for nasolacrimal duct obstruction
what does mucopurulent fluid from the puncta mean
when should you not do the tear duct test
cards.x: Have the patient look up. Then press on the lower lid near the medial canthus (the inner corner of the eye), just inside the bony rim, to compress the lacrimal sac. Look for fluid regurgitating from the puncta (the small tear openings). Mucopurulent fluid means obstruction. Avoid the test if the area is significantly inflamed or tender.

cards.t: Everting the upper lid to find a foreign body
q: how do you evert the upper eyelid
when should you not evert the eyelid
how do you find a foreign body under the lid
cards.x: The patient looks down and relaxes. Raise the lid so the lashes protrude, grasp them and pull down and forward. Place a stick at least 1 centimeter above the lid margin, at the upper border of the tarsal plate, and push down as you raise the lid edge. Do not press on the eyeball. Never evert if globe rupture is suspected.

cards.t: Comparing the common causes of a red eye
q: how do you tell conjunctivitis from iritis and glaucoma
what is ciliary injection
how do you compare the causes of a red eye
what does a painless red eye mean
cards.x:
Five causes of a red eye differ in pattern of redness, pain, vision, discharge, pupil and cornea. In order:

- Conjunctivitis: diffuse redness, maximal peripherally (conjunctival injection). Mild discomfort, vision only briefly blurred by discharge, watery, mucoid or mucopurulent discharge, normal pupil, clear cornea.
- Corneal injury or infection: moderate to severe superficial pain, usually decreased vision, watery or purulent discharge, pupil normal unless iritis develops, cornea changes with the cause.
- Acute iritis: moderate, aching, deep pain, decreased vision, no discharge, a pupil that may be small and, with time, irregular, cornea clear or slightly clouded.
- Acute glaucoma: severe, aching, deep pain, decreased vision, no discharge, a dilated fixed pupil, and a steamy cloudy cornea. It is an emergency, from an acute rise in eye pressure.
- Subconjunctival hemorrhage: no pain, normal vision and pupil, no discharge, clear cornea, with a sharply demarcated red area.

cards.t: Spotting the dangerous red eye when the redness pattern doesn't help
q: how do you recognize a dangerous red eye
what is ciliary injection
what are the warning signs in a red eye
cards.x:
Ciliary injection is deeper vessels visible as radiating vessels, or a reddish-violet flush around the limbus (the edge of the cornea). It is an important sign of corneal injury, acute iritis and acute glaucoma, the three dangerous causes. But those eyes can also look diffusely red instead.

When the injection pattern does not help, four backup clues catch the dangerous three: pain, decreased vision, unequal pupils, and a less than perfectly clear (hazy) cornea.

cards.t: Subconjunctival hemorrhage
k: red patch on white of eye
q: what is a subconjunctival hemorrhage
is a subconjunctival hemorrhage painful
when does a subconjunctival hemorrhage suggest globe rupture
cards.x:
A subconjunctival hemorrhage is leakage of blood outside the vessels: a homogeneous, sharply demarcated red area that fades to yellow then disappears. It is the cause of a red eye with no pain, no discharge, an unaffected pupil and vision, and a clear cornea. It often has no significance, but it may result from trauma, bleeding disorders, or a sudden increase in venous pressure such as coughing.

After trauma, globe rupture is more likely, especially when the hemorrhage encircles the entire cornea.

cards.t: Blepharitis and nodular episcleritis
q: what is blepharitis
what diseases are linked to nodular episcleritis
what is blepharitis associated with
cards.x: Blepharitis is a common eye inflammation. It is associated with bacterial infection and atopic dermatitis. Nodular episcleritis can be seen in rheumatoid arthritis and lupus erythematosus. So a nodular red spot on the eye can be a clue to one of those diseases.

cards.t: Visual acuity (20/200) and the eye abbreviations
k: counting fingers hand motion light perception
q: what do OD, OS and OU mean
what does 20/200 vision mean
how do you record vision when the patient cannot read the chart
cards.x:
OD (the right eye), OS (the left eye) and OU (both eyes) are terms you must remember. Visual acuity is written as a fraction: 20/200 means that at 20 feet the patient reads print that a normal eye reads at 200 feet. The larger the second number, the worse the vision.

If the patient cannot read the chart, document counting fingers, hand motion, or light perception.

cards.t: The pinhole test
q: what does the pinhole test show
why does a pinhole improve vision
what if the pinhole doesn't improve vision
cards.x:
The pinhole test tells a refractive error (a focusing problem) from other causes of poor vision. The pinhole blocks the scattered outer rays and lets through only a narrow central beam. That shrinks the blur, so vision improves if the problem is a refractive error.

If vision is not corrected with the pinhole, consider cataract, optic nerve disease or retinal disease.

cards.t: Confrontation visual field testing
q: how do you test visual fields by confrontation
what is the static finger wiggle test
where is the normal blind spot
what does an enlarged blind spot mean
cards.x:
Confrontation fields are best done with both of two tests:

- The static finger wiggle test: at arm's length, hands about two feet apart lateral to the ears, wiggling fingers are brought slowly into view, testing each quadrant.
- The kinetic red target test: a 5 millimeter red-topped pin is moved inward from beyond each quadrant, and you ask when it first appears red.

A temporal defect in one eye should prompt testing for a nasal defect in the other. The normal blind spot sits 15 degrees temporal to the line of gaze and is enlarged in glaucoma, optic neuritis and papilledema.

cards.t: Nystagmus, lid lag and the cover-uncover test
q: what is nystagmus
is nystagmus always abnormal
what is lid lag
what does the cover-uncover test show
cards.x:
Nystagmus is a fine rhythmic oscillation of the eyes. A few beats on lateral gaze is normal; bring the finger back into binocular vision (both eyes working together), and if it persists there, consider a neurologic condition.

Lid lag, where sclera is visible above the iris on downgaze, is most often hyperthyroidism. The cover-uncover test reveals slight muscle imbalance not otherwise seen.

cards.t: Unequal pupils (anisocoria) and the near reaction
q: when are unequal pupils normal
what size difference in pupils is abnormal
which nerve controls pupil constriction for near
cards.x:
A difference in pupil size of half to one millimeter is common, and anisocoria (unequal pupils) is benign if the reactions are normal. Abnormal is a difference greater than 1 millimeter, or a poorly reactive pupil.

The constriction that happens when the eyes focus on a near object (the near reaction) is mediated by the oculomotor nerve. Convergence and accommodation happen alongside it but are not part of it.

cards.t: A dilated pupil: the emergency and the three causes
q: why is an acute dilated pupil an emergency
what causes a dilated pupil
what causes a fixed dilated pupil
cards.x:
An acute, significantly dilated pupil is a medical emergency, particularly with headache or other neurologic signs. The worries are uncal herniation (the brain being pushed out of place) or a posterior communicating artery aneurysm causing a third nerve palsy.

Once local eye disease is excluded, only three causes of a dilated pupil remain:

- compression or other lesion of cranial nerve III
- parasympathetic denervation from a ciliary ganglion lesion (Adie's pupil)
- pharmacologic block of the pupillary sphincter (the muscle that constricts the pupil)

cards.t: The swinging light test and the relative afferent pupillary defect
q: what is the swinging light test
what is a relative afferent pupillary defect
what is a Marcus Gunn pupil
why does the pupil dilate when light swings to it
cards.x:
The swinging light test is indicated for anisocoria and assesses functional impairment of the optic nerve and the integrity of the visual pathways. Normally both pupils constrict when light shines in one eye (the direct and consensual responses).

Abnormal is paradoxical dilation of both pupils when the light swings to the affected eye, with an intact consensual reflex. That is a relative afferent pupillary defect (a Marcus Gunn pupil), and the lesion is the optic nerve. The mechanism: the afferent stimulus on that side is reduced, so the efferent signal to both pupils falls and a net dilation results.

cards.t: Adie's tonic pupil
q: what is Adie's pupil
how does Adie's pupil react to light
why does Adie's pupil blur near vision
cards.x:
Adie's tonic pupil is a large, regular pupil, usually in one eye. Its reaction to light is severely reduced and slowed, or absent. The reaction to near is present but very slow.

The cause is degeneration of the ciliary ganglia and postganglionic parasympathetic fibers, and the slow accommodation blurs near vision. It is one of the causes of a dilated pupil with the parasympathetic nerve supply cut.

cards.t: Argyll Robertson pupil
q: what is an Argyll Robertson pupil
what causes an Argyll Robertson pupil
how does an Argyll Robertson pupil react
cards.x:
The Argyll Robertson pupil is small, unequal and irregular. It does not react to light but it does constrict for near: "accommodates but doesn't react".

It is classically from tertiary syphilis (neurosyphilis); diabetes and Lyme disease can cause a similar pupil, and today diabetes is the more common cause of a similar picture. Mydriatics (drops that dilate the pupil) dilate it only incompletely.

cards.t: Horner syndrome
q: what is Horner syndrome
what are the signs of Horner syndrome
what is the pupil like in Horner syndrome
cards.x:
Horner syndrome gives a small pupil (miosis) that reacts briskly to both light and near. It comes with ptosis (a droopy lid) and anhidrosis (no sweating) on the same side of the face. This happens because the sympathetic supply to the pupil and to the lid muscle is interrupted.

In the congenital form, the involved iris is lighter in color (heterochromia).

cards.t: The pupil in oculomotor (third nerve) palsy
q: what does the pupil look like in an oculomotor palsy
what signs accompany a third nerve palsy
how do you tell oculomotor palsy from Horner syndrome
cards.x:
In a compressive oculomotor palsy the pupil is dilated and fixed to both light and near; in a diabetic (ischemic) palsy the pupil is often spared. Ptosis and a lateral deviation of the eye are almost always present.

Compare Horner syndrome, where the pupil is small and reacts briskly: a dilated, fixed pupil with ptosis points to the oculomotor nerve, while a small, reactive pupil with ptosis points to the sympathetic supply.

cards.t: The oblique lighting (crescent shadow) test
q: what is the crescent shadow test
how do you check for a narrow angle
what does a shadow on the iris mean
how do you tell a corneal scar from a cataract
cards.x:
Oblique lighting assesses the depth of the anterior chamber angle. Shine light from the temporal side and look for a shadow on the medial iris.

No shadow is normal: the iris is flat and the angle is open. A shadow means the iris is bowed forward into a narrow angle, which raises the risk of narrow-angle glaucoma.

A corneal scar is a superficial grayish-white opacity. Do not confuse it with a cataract, which lies deeper and is seen only through the pupil.

cards.t: When not to dilate the pupils
q: when should you not dilate the pupils
what do you document when you dilate
how long does a weak mydriatic last
cards.x:
Do not dilate if:

- serial neurologic examinations are required
- the patient is elderly and has had no cataract surgery (a thick natural lens can crowd the angle)
- acute angle-closure glaucoma is suspected

If you do dilate, document the time and the agents used. A weak mydriatic reverses in 4 to 6 hours.

cards.t: The optic disc: normal, papilledema, cupping and atrophy
q: what does papilledema look like
what is glaucomatous cupping
what does optic atrophy look like
what does a normal optic disc look like
cards.x:
The normal disc has a sharp margin and small disc vessels, and the cup sits centrally or slightly temporal with a diameter less than half the disc.

- Papilledema (a sign of raised intracranial pressure): the disc is pink and swollen with blurred margins; the cup is not visible and vessel pulsations are lost.
- Glaucomatous cupping: the cup is enlarged, more than half the disc, and the vessels sink in and around the disc.
- Optic atrophy: the disc is white and the tiny disc vessels are absent. It is seen in optic neuritis, multiple sclerosis and temporal arteritis.

cards.t: Orbital (blow-out) fracture and enophthalmos
q: what are the signs of an orbital blow-out fracture
why does a blow-out fracture cause double vision on upward gaze
what is enophthalmos
cards.x:
An orbital (blow-out) fracture causes:

- a sunken eye
- hypoesthesia (decreased sensation) of the infraorbital area, from the infraorbital nerve
- diplopia, particularly on upward gaze
- decreased motility
- sometimes a nosebleed on the same side (ipsilateral)

Refer to ophthalmology or oral and maxillofacial surgery.

Mechanism matters, and so does the size of the object. Larger objects transfer most of their energy to the orbital rim, while smaller ones may strike the globe directly.

Enophthalmos is the sunken eye, with ecchymosis (bruising), point tenderness and a palpable step-off at the orbital rim. Observe from above the head, looking down.

cards.t: Zygomatic fracture
q: what are the signs of a zygomatic fracture
how do you look for malar flattening
why does a zygomatic fracture hurt when opening the mouth
cards.x:
A zygomatic fracture shows as flattening of the malar eminence (the cheekbone prominence), best seen from behind the seated patient looking down. There is edema and ecchymosis of the temple or infraorbital area, a palpable step-off at the zygoma, and infraorbital hypoesthesia.

Pain on opening the mouth is a clue, because the temporalis muscle passes medial to the arch and inserts on the mandible.

cards.t: Hyphema
q: what is a hyphema
how do you evaluate a hyphema
what causes a hyphema
cards.x: A hyphema is blood in the anterior chamber of the eye, usually from blunt trauma. Evaluate it by checking acuity, the pupils, the red reflex, the intraocular pressure and the slit lamp. In the pupils, look for a crescent-like iris defect if the iris is torn, and reduced reactions if the sphincter is damaged.

cards.t: Corneal abrasion
q: what is a corneal abrasion
what are the signs of a corneal abrasion
should you give a topical anesthetic for a corneal abrasion
why evert the eyelid in a corneal abrasion
cards.x:
A corneal abrasion is a scratch on the cornea, from blunt trauma such as a fingernail or a contact lens. The patient has significant pain, photophobia, blepharospasm (squeezing the lid shut), a foreign body sensation and tearing.

Evert the upper lid: a foreign body in the upper tarsal conjunctiva scratches the cornea with every blink. A hazy cornea suggests a bacterial infection. A topical anesthetic gives immediate relief but is for diagnosis, not treatment.

cards.t: Corneal ulcer and fluorescein staining
q: what is a corneal ulcer
what does fluorescein show
why is a herpes corneal ulcer not very painful
how do you see a corneal ulcer
cards.x:
A corneal ulcer causes pain, photophobia, tearing and reduced vision. The eye is red with circumcorneal injection (redness around the cornea) and purulent or watery discharge. Herpes simplex ulcers are not very painful.

To see it, an ophthalmoscope set at plus 40 diopters acts as a magnifying lens, but fluorescein is more sensitive for early ulcers. Fluorescein is an orange dye instilled in the eye and viewed under blue light; it is taken up by areas of cornea devoid of epithelium.

cards.t: Eye problems that need urgent action (disposition)
q: which eye problems are emergencies
which eye problems go to ophthalmology immediately
what do you do for a chemical burn of the eye
cards.x:
These are the eye problems to recognize when deciding where a patient goes next. They are sudden vision loss, retinal artery occlusion, chemical burns, rupture, acute angle-closure glaucoma, vitreous hemorrhage, orbital cellulitis, corneal ulcer or abrasion, retinal detachment, macular edema or hemorrhage, and hyphema.

A chemical burn is emergent. Irrigate the eye at once, then send the patient to ophthalmology immediately. So do rupture and sudden vision loss.

cards.t: Remembering Weber and Rinne
q: how do I remember Weber versus Rinne
which ear does Weber point to in conductive loss
where does the Rinne tuning fork go
cards.x:
Two memory tricks keep the tests straight.

- "Rinne is under the pinna." The outside of the ear is the pinna; the Rinne fork goes on the mastoid, under it. So anything placed under the ear is Rinne.
- "Weber tells you whether." Weber tells you whether it is the right ear or the left.

For the two kinds of hearing loss: in sensorineural loss, Weber goes to the good ear. In conductive loss, it goes to the ear that is blocked.

cards.t: The ear history: referred ear pain and associated symptoms
q: why can ear pain come from outside the ear
which nerves refer pain to the ear
how do you start the ear history
what is OPPQRST
cards.x:
The ear history opens with one question, "Have you had any trouble with your ears?", and then splits four ways: pain, discharge, hearing, and the vertigo and tinnitus group.

Pain is the one that misleads, because the ear may be entirely normal. Ear pain is frequently referred; the sources to ask about are the temporomandibular joint, the teeth and the cervical spine, carried by cranial nerves V, VII, IX and X. Four sensory nerves supply one small structure, which is why disease well away from the ear arrives as otalgia (ear pain). Don't go with the first answer; keep asking, because a wrong history leads to the wrong exam, diagnosis and treatment.

Also ask about fever, sore throat, cough and upper respiratory infection, and keep otitis media, otitis externa and eustachian tube dysfunction in mind as local causes. The history structure is OPPQRST (onset, palliative, provoking, quality, radiation, site, timing).

cards.t: Ear discharge: what to ask and what it points to
q: what causes ear discharge
how do you characterize ear discharge
what does ear discharge point to
cards.x:
Discharge from the ear is characterized by color, consistency and quantity. The possibilities are cerumen, blood, water or purulent (pus) fluid.

It points to otitis externa, otitis media with perforation (a hole in the eardrum), or trauma and foreign bodies.

cards.t: Asking about hearing: volume versus clarity
k: do you have difficulty understanding people
q: how do you ask about hearing loss
why do noisy places help conductive hearing loss
what question separates conductive from sensorineural loss
cards.x:
Start with "How is your hearing?" Then ask "Do you have difficulty understanding people when they speak?" The second question is the useful one. It separates volume from clarity:

- Trouble understanding speech, others seem to mumble: sensorineural.
- Worse in noisy environments: sensorineural.
- Noisy environments may help: conductive.

Why noise can help in conductive loss: the block turns everything down, including the background (it attenuates, or reduces, it). It does not change the balance of speech and noise. But everyone around the patient raises their voice over that background, so the louder speech still gets through even though the noise is also turned down.

cards.t: "Dizziness": vertigo, presyncope, disequilibrium or psychiatric
q: what does a patient mean by dizzy
how do you sort out dizziness
what is the difference between vertigo and presyncope
cards.x:
"Dizziness" means nothing until the patient explains it. It is very important to have the patient explain the term, and it splits four ways:

- Vertigo: a spinning sensation.
- Presyncope: faint or lightheaded.
- Disequilibrium: unsteadiness or imbalance.
- Psychiatric: anxiety, depression, alcohol or other substances.

Four patients can use one word for four unrelated problems, so one clarifying question changes the whole workup.

cards.t: Tinnitus, vertigo and ototoxic medications in the ear history
q: what is tinnitus
what is vertigo
which medications should you ask about in a hearing history
cards.x:
Tinnitus is sound with no external source. Unexplained tinnitus stands alone; tinnitus with hearing loss and vertigo points to Ménière disease. Vertigo is the perception of rotation, spinning or tilting, and points to inner ear problems: labyrinthitis, cranial nerve VIII, benign positional vertigo, Ménière disease.

Ask about medications: aminoglycosides, aspirin, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, quinine and furosemide. All five are common, and none of them will be volunteered by the patient.

cards.t: Comparing the causes of vertigo
q: how do you tell the causes of vertigo apart
which causes of vertigo affect hearing
how long does each type of vertigo last
cards.x:
Six causes of vertigo can be separated by reading the duration first, then checking hearing and tinnitus. The two together narrow the list a lot, and neurologic signs then separate central vertigo.

Hearing is the great divider: of the six, only Ménière disease, drug toxicity and acoustic neuroma touch it. Benign positional vertigo and vestibular neuronitis leave hearing alone. Central vertigo has no ear symptoms and plenty of neurological ones.

- Benign positional vertigo: seconds to under a minute per attack.
- Vestibular neuronitis: hours to two weeks.
- Ménière disease: several hours to a day or more, recurrent, with fluctuating tinnitus and a sensorineural loss.
- Acoustic neuroma: impairs hearing in one ear, with tinnitus.

cards.t: Benign positional vertigo
q: what is benign positional vertigo
how long does an episode of benign positional vertigo last
what triggers benign positional vertigo
cards.x:
Benign positional vertigo is a peripheral cause of vertigo. It comes on suddenly with a change in position, such as rolling onto the affected side or tilting the head up. Each attack lasts seconds to under a minute. The condition itself lasts a few weeks and may recur. Hearing is not affected and tinnitus is absent. There may be nausea, vomiting and nystagmus (jerking eye movements).

Notice that positional vertigo is defined by how brief each episode is. Episode length and illness length are different numbers: seconds for the attack, weeks for the condition.

cards.t: Vestibular neuronitis (acute labyrinthitis)
q: what is vestibular neuronitis
how long does vestibular neuronitis last
does vestibular neuronitis affect hearing
cards.x:
Vestibular neuronitis is a peripheral cause of vertigo that begins suddenly and lasts hours to two weeks; it may recur over 12 to 18 months. Hearing is not affected and tinnitus is absent in vestibular neuronitis; if hearing loss or tinnitus comes with the vertigo, think labyrinthitis instead. Patients have nausea, vomiting and nystagmus.

Compared with benign positional vertigo, the clue is duration: hours to weeks rather than seconds.

cards.t: Central vertigo
q: what is central vertigo
how do you tell central from peripheral vertigo
what neurologic signs come with central vertigo
cards.x:
Central vertigo is vertigo from the brain rather than the ear. It is often sudden, and causes include a brainstem lesion, atherosclerosis, multiple sclerosis, vertebrobasilar migraine and transient ischemic attack. Duration is variable, from brief spells (as in a transient ischemic attack) to constant vertigo lasting days (as in a stroke).

Hearing is not affected and there is no tinnitus. The pattern is no ear symptoms and plenty of neurological ones: other brainstem deficits such as dysarthria (slurred speech), ataxia (poor coordination), and crossed motor and sensory deficits.

cards.t: Inspecting and palpating the ear before the otoscope
q: what do you do before using the otoscope
what is microtia
what are tophi on the ear
why palpate the tragus and mastoid first
cards.x:
Inspect and palpate before the otoscope: the auricles, the mastoid and the tragus. Tenderness localizes disease before anything enters the canal.

Two findings to know. Microtia is an abnormally small, congenitally underdeveloped auricle, grouped with atresia among the congenital deformities. Hard nodules on the auricle made of uric acid crystals are tophi, indicating chronic tophaceous gout; they are deposits rather than growths, and on the ear they point to long-standing disease.

cards.t: Otoscopy technique: why each step matters
k: pull the auricle up and back
q: how do you hold an otoscope
why pull the ear up and back
why use the largest speculum
why rest your hand on the patient's head
cards.x:
Every element of otoscopy earns its place.

- Pull the auricle up, back and away from the head. This straightens the canal; the view is only as good as the alignment.
- Use the largest speculum that will fit. A small one leaks, and insufflation needs a seal.
- The ulnar aspect of your hand (the pinky side) contacts the patient. This anchors the instrument to the head, so a sudden movement takes the otoscope with it rather than into the canal.
- Insufflate (puff air in): reduced mobility means an effusion or a thickened membrane.

You have to see hundreds of normal eardrums before you see anything abnormal: find the handle of the malleus and the cone of light, so you notice when they are missing.

cards.t: Doing pneumatic insufflation properly
q: how do you do pneumatic otoscopy
how do you check an otoscope for leaks
why might the eardrum look immobile
cards.x:
After attaching the speculum, check the otoscope for leaks: place a finger over the speculum tip and squeeze the bulb. You should feel pressure build if there is no leak. Then insert it, confirm the seal, and apply quick, firm but gentle pressure while you watch the membrane.

Without a seal the test is not merely harder, it is inaccurate: an immobile-looking drum may just be a leaking instrument. Reduced mobility on insufflation points to an effusion behind the membrane or to a thickened tympanic membrane.

cards.t: Ear canal findings: wax, foreign bodies, acute versus chronic otitis externa
q: what can you find in the ear canal
how do acute and chronic otitis externa look different
what foreign bodies are found in the ear
cards.x:
In the canal you may find cerumen and foreign bodies. The list of things that end up there, under "if it fits", includes Q-tips, beads, pencil lead, styrofoam, crayons, popcorn and tympanostomy tubes.

Otitis externa comes in two forms:

- Acute otitis externa: the canal is swollen, narrow, moist, pale and tender (it may be erythematous).
- Chronic otitis externa: the canal skin is thickened, red and itchy.

Acute versus chronic is pain versus itch, and swelling versus thickening. The distinction is easier from the history than from the picture.

cards.t: Eardrum perforation and tympanosclerosis
q: what is the difference between central and marginal perforation
what is tympanosclerosis
is tympanosclerosis significant
cards.x:
A perforation (a hole in the eardrum) is central if it does not extend to the margin, and marginal if it involves the margin. It is usually secondary to otitis media, and there may be drainage through it.

Tympanosclerosis is a hyaline (glassy scar-like) deposit in the membrane. It is left after severe otitis media or a healed perforation, including grommet (ventilation tube) sites. It is usually not clinically significant.

cards.t: Serous effusion, otitis media and bullous myringitis on the eardrum
q: what does a serous effusion look like
what is bullous myringitis
what does otitis media look like on the eardrum
cards.x:
Three eardrum pictures to tell apart:

- Serous effusion: amber fluid, sometimes with bubbles. It follows an upper respiratory infection or a change in atmospheric pressure.
- Otitis media: red, landmarks lost, bulging, with purulent (pus) effusion. Two common bacteria are Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae.
- Bullous myringitis: painful hemorrhagic vesicles (blood-filled blisters) on the membrane or canal. It may be viral or bacterial.

cards.t: Bulging of the eardrum is graded
q: how do you grade a bulging eardrum
when do the landmarks disappear in otitis media
why does the grade of bulging matter
cards.x:
Bulging is graded, not binary. A four-panel series runs from normal (A) through mild (B) and moderate (C) to severe (D) bulging from middle ear effusion.

The useful part is the middle two: a mildly bulging drum still has landmarks you can pick out. The point at which the landmarks disappear is the point at which the effusion has become convincing.

cards.t: The whispered voice test and other bedside hearing screens
q: how do you do the whispered voice test
why stand behind the patient for the whisper test
what are the bedside hearing screens
cards.x:
For the whispered voice test, stand two feet behind the patient (which removes lip reading), occlude the ear not being tested, and whisper a three-number or letter sequence twice. Normal is three or more of six correct; abnormal is four of six incorrect.

The other bedside screens are the finger rub and a watch.

cards.t: Conductive versus sensorineural hearing loss compared
k: why do people with sensorineural loss talk loudly
q: what is the difference between conductive and sensorineural hearing loss
why is the voice soft in conductive loss
why does a patient with sensorineural loss speak loudly
how does noise affect each type
cards.x:
Conductive loss is a problem in the external or middle ear that impairs conduction to the inner ear. Sensorineural loss is a problem in the inner ear involving the cochlear nerve and impulse transmission to the brain.

- Age: conductive begins in childhood and young adulthood, up to about 40; sensorineural in the middle or later years.
- Canal and drum: in conductive loss the abnormality is usually visible (except in otosclerosis); in sensorineural loss the problem is not visible.
- Noise: conductive loss has little effect on sound, and hearing seems to improve in a noisy environment; in sensorineural loss the higher registers are lost, sound may be distorted, and hearing worsens in noise.
- Voice: in conductive loss it stays soft, because the inner ear and nerve are intact; in sensorineural loss it may be loud, because hearing is difficult. A patient who cannot hear themselves speaks up.

cards.t: The Weber test
q: what is the Weber test
what does Weber show in conductive hearing loss
what does Weber show in sensorineural hearing loss
what is a normal Weber
cards.x:
In the Weber test, the base of the fork is placed on the top of the head or mid-forehead (the vertex). The test evaluates unilateral hearing loss by lateralization, meaning which ear hears it better.

- Normal: the sound is heard at the midline, or equally in both ears.
- Conductive loss: it lateralizes to the impaired ear. Room noise is not well heard there, so detection of vibration improves.
- Sensorineural loss: it lateralizes to the good ear, because damage impairs transmission on the affected side.

cards.t: The Rinne test
q: what is the Rinne test
what does Rinne show in conductive loss
why is Rinne normal in sensorineural loss
how do you perform the Rinne test
cards.x:
In the Rinne test, you place the fork on the mastoid until the sound stops, then beside the canal, and ask whether it is still heard. It compares air conduction (through the canal, drum and ossicles) with bone conduction (straight through the skull).

- Normal and sensorineural loss: air conduction is greater than bone conduction.
- Conductive loss: bone conduction is equal to or greater than air conduction, because vibration through bone bypasses the blocked external or middle ear to reach the cochlea.

The sensorineural result is the counterintuitive one. Rinne compares two routes to the same cochlea. Damage the cochlea and both routes degrade together, so the ratio is unchanged: a "normal" Rinne in an ear that hears badly. That is the test working, not failing.

cards.t: A worked example: Weber and Rinne together
q: how do you interpret Weber and Rinne together
Rinne normal on the right and Weber to the right means which ear is affected
cards.x:
Take this case. On the right, the Rinne shows sound heard better in the air (normal). The Weber is heard better in the right ear. Which ear has sensorineural loss?

The left. The normal Rinne rules out a conductive problem on the right. The Weber sound shifts away from a sensorineural lesion (it lateralizes), so hearing it on the right puts the damage on the left.

The method is to use Rinne to say whether each ear is conductively normal, then use Weber to see which side is the odd one out.

cards.t: What tuning forks cannot tell you
q: what are the limits of tuning fork tests
can tuning forks detect bilateral hearing loss
what tuning fork do you use for hearing tests
cards.x:
Use a 512 hertz fork, the smaller one, in a quiet room. That frequency sits in the speech range and rings long enough to compare two positions.

The tests have limits. They do not distinguish normal from bilateral sensorineural loss, and they do not distinguish normal from mixed conductive and sensorineural loss. Both tests work by comparing, one side against the other or one route against the other. A loss that is symmetrical, or that hits both routes, leaves the comparison looking normal.

cards.t: Common causes of conductive and sensorineural hearing loss
q: what causes conductive hearing loss
what causes sensorineural hearing loss
what are exostoses
why does presbycusis cause trouble understanding words
cards.x:
Conductive causes include cerumen, foreign bodies, effusions, exostoses, tumors, eardrum perforation, otitis media and otosclerosis of the ossicles. They obstruct or load the external or middle ear. Exostoses are benign bony growths in the ear canal that narrow it mechanically.

Sensorineural causes include loud noise, inner ear infection, trauma, acoustic neuroma, congenital and familial disorders, and aging. Rubella and cytomegalovirus both damage the inner ear, and both matter most when the exposure was congenital.

Presbycusis is a higher-frequency loss, so the complaint is about clarity rather than volume, because the high registers carry the consonants.

cards.t: Nose and sinus anatomy: why the drainage explains the disease
q: where does the maxillary sinus drain
how many turbinates are there
why are ear, nose and throat problems connected
why be aggressive with infections near the sinuses
cards.x:
There are three turbinates (shelf-like structures inside the nose): the superior, middle and inferior. The maxillary sinus drains at the middle turbinate. The eustachian tube opens into the back of the nose (the nasopharynx), which is why ear, nose and throat problems travel together; tears also drain into the nose through the nasolacrimal duct, which is why you get congestion when you cry.

The warning that goes with it: the sinuses and the top of the nose sit just beneath the base of the skull, so infection there can spread upward toward the brain. Any infection in this area deserves a more aggressive approach.

cards.t: The nose and sinus history
q: what do you ask in a nose and sinus history
why ask about dental work with sinus symptoms
why ask about cocaine in nasal complaints
cards.x:
Ask about onset and duration, sick contacts and recent travel. Ask about recent dental work, because dental work can affect the maxillary sinuses, which sit directly above the upper tooth roots. Seasonal or environmental triggers point to allergic rhinitis, and facial pain or tenderness points to sinusitis. Ask about medications, including duration and efficacy, and specifically rhinitis medicamentosa and cocaine. Ask whether the sense of smell is affected.

Epistaxis (nosebleed) is caused by digital trauma or other trauma, inflammation, dry mucosa, a foreign body, or a tumor. Recurrent bleeding, or bleeding and bruising elsewhere, suggests a systemic problem; one nosebleed is local until a pattern says otherwise.

cards.t: Inspecting the inside of the nose
q: how do you test nasal patency
what does unilateral nasal obstruction suggest
what are nasal polyps associated with
what does the nasal lining look like in viral versus allergic rhinitis
cards.x:
Inspecting the inside of the nose covers patency, masses, shape, discharge, lining and septum:

- Patency: occlude one nostril and breathe in. Unilateral obstruction suggests a foreign body, tumor or deviated septum.
- Masses: polyps are associated with allergic rhinitis, aspirin sensitivity, asthma, chronic sinus infection and cystic fibrosis. Also cysts and tumors.
- Symmetry and deformity: deviated septum, perforated septum, trauma.
- Discharge: thick and purulent, thin and watery, or bloody. Note the odor.
- Mucosa (lining): look at color, swelling, bleeding and ulceration. Red and swollen suggests viral; pale, bluish or red suggests allergic.
- Septum: perforation comes from trauma, surgery or drug use.

cards.t: Palpating and transilluminating the sinuses
q: how do you examine the sinuses
how do you transilluminate the sinuses
what does absence of glow mean
is transillumination reliable
cards.x:
For palpation, press up on the frontal sinuses, avoiding the eyes, and press up on the maxillary sinuses.

For transillumination, use a dark room. For the frontal sinus, put the light up under the brow close to the nose. For the maxillary sinus, put the light down just below the inner corner of the eye, with the mouth open. Absence of glow suggests thickened mucosa or secretions, but the test is not sensitive or specific.

cards.t: Polyp or boggy turbinate? Identify before you pull
q: how do you tell a nasal polyp from a turbinate
why not pull on a nasal mass
what is the common error with nasal polyps
cards.x:
A nasal polyp is a pale, grape-like, mobile growth.
