It usually comes from higher up in the nose and can hang down between the septum and the inferior turbinate (a shelf-like structure on the side wall of the nose). In allergic rhinitis, the turbinate itself looks swollen and boggy and is fixed to the wall. The common error is mistaking an allergic-looking, boggy inferior turbinate for a polyp.

Don't pull what you haven't identified. Imaging once showed that a lesion everyone had called a polyp was brain tissue coming through. You need to know what you are looking at before you start pulling things. If you're not sure, be careful.

cards.t: What is and isn't diagnostic in acute sinusitis
q: does purulent discharge mean bacterial sinusitis
how long before sinusitis is bacterial
what suggests acute sinusitis
cards.x:
Local tenderness, pain, fever and nasal discharge are suggestive of acute sinusitis. So is purulent discharge. But the color of the discharge is not diagnostic. Purulent discharge doesn't need to be there, and it isn't proof.

Acute bacterial sinusitis is unlikely with symptoms under 7 days, unless the onset is severe. Severe means a fever of 39 degrees Celsius or higher with purulent discharge or facial pain for 3 to 4 days in a row at the start. It takes time to develop, so a short illness is much more likely to be viral.

cards.t: Septal hematoma
q: what is a septal hematoma
why must a septal hematoma be drained
what happens if septal hematoma is not treated
cards.x:
A septal hematoma is the nose finding that cannot wait. Injury disrupts the blood vessels and pulls the lining away from the cartilage, so blood collects between the lining and the cartilage. It requires urgent drainage to prevent necrosis of the septal cartilage. The cartilage has no blood supply of its own and depends entirely on the lining that has just been stripped off it.

The rule is broader than the nose: a hematoma (collection of blood) in the ear has to be drained too, just like one in the nose.

cards.t: Deviated septum: airflow matters, not appearance
q: does a deviated septum always cause obstruction
how do you assess a deviated septum
what matters in a deviated septum
cards.x: A deviated septum may be entirely asymptomatic. The outside appearance can be striking with little obstruction behind it, and the reverse is also true. What matters is airflow, not appearance, so test patency rather than trusting the profile.

cards.t: The oral cavity: anatomy and history
q: what are the parts of the oral cavity
what do you ask in a mouth and throat history
what causes hoarseness
what does a sore smooth tongue suggest
cards.x:
The oral cavity is named in order: medial incisor, lateral incisor, canine, premolars and molars; then the hard palate, the soft palate and uvula, the tonsils between the anterior and posterior pillars, the pharynx behind, and the buccal mucosa (the cheek lining).

The history asks about a sore throat (which brings in the Centor rule); a sore tongue (aphthous ulcers, or a nutritional deficiency if it is sore and smooth); bleeding gums (gingivitis); hoarseness (viral laryngitis, overuse, laryngeal nerve damage, reflux, smoking); swollen glands or lumps in the neck; and tobacco and alcohol use.

cards.t: Oral examination findings: lips, pharynx, uvula and teeth
q: what do you look for in the oral exam
what does uvula deviation mean
why remove dentures in the oral exam
what is angular cheilitis
cards.x:
The oral examination looks at the lips, the mucosa, tonsils and pharynx, the uvula and soft palate, and the teeth:

- Lips: color, texture, cracks and sores. Angular cheilitis is at the corners; also angioedema (swelling) and herpes simplex.
- Mucosa, tonsils and pharynx: erythema, exudates, ulcerations, lesions. The posterior pharynx may need a tongue blade.
- Uvula and soft palate: failure to rise, with deviation of the uvula to the opposite side, means cranial nerve X paralysis.
- Dentition: caries (cavities) and erosions. Look under dentures for ulcers and lesions; a denture hides the mucosa most at risk from chronic irritation, so dentures are removed.

cards.t: Examining the tongue and palpating the mouth
q: what do you look for on the tongue
where does tongue cancer occur
why switch hands when palpating the tongue
what is geographic tongue
cards.x:
Look at the tongue's texture, color and lesions. A smooth, beefy red tongue suggests vitamin B-12 deficiency. Tongue cancers sit typically on the lateral border or the undersurface, look indurated (firm) red or white, and are seen in males over 50. Geographic tongue is benign: a map-like pattern of patches, and recognizing it mostly avoids mistaking it for something that needs investigation. Asymmetric protrusion suggests a cranial nerve XII lesion.

For palpation, feel the floor of the mouth, then the tongue: hold it with gauze in one hand and palpate with the other, then switch hands for the opposite side. Switching hands is the only way to reach both lateral borders properly, and the lateral border and undersurface are exactly where the cancers are.

cards.t: Other mouth findings: Vincent's angina, torus palatinus
q: what is Vincent's angina
what is torus palatinus
what causes trench mouth
cards.x:
Necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis, also called Vincent's angina or trench mouth, comes from poor dental hygiene and drug use. The bacteria keep growing and destroy tissue as they go, and the smell can be noticeable from across the room.

Torus palatinus is a benign midline bony growth on the hard palate. Streptococcal pharyngitis gives erythematous tonsils, often with exudate, and candidal pharyngitis is its own picture. Aphthous ulcers round out the findings.

cards.t: The modified Centor score and the chance of strep
q: what is the chance of strep at each Centor score
what does a Centor score of 3 mean
what does a Centor score of 0 mean
cards.x:
The modified Centor score gives each patient a rough chance of group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis (strep throat):

- Score of 0 or less: about 1 to 2.5 percent.
- Score of 1: 5 to 10 percent.
- Score of 2: 11 to 17 percent.
- Score of 3: 28 to 35 percent.
- Score of 4 or more: 51 to 53 percent.

The Centor rule is a clinical prediction rule: it converts findings into a probability and a course of action. A score of 0 or less needs no further testing or antibiotics, and the scores in between go to throat culture or rapid antigen detection.

cards.t: The neck lymph node chains and how to palpate them
q: what are the lymph node chains of the head and neck
in what order do you palpate the neck nodes
how do you palpate lymph nodes
cards.x: Palpate the node chains in a fixed order: preauricular, postauricular, occipital, tonsillar, submandibular, submental, superficial (anterior) cervical, posterior cervical, deep cervical, and supraclavicular. Use the pads of the index and middle fingers. Following a fixed route is what stops one being missed, and each chain should be named as it is palpated.

cards.t: What lymph node characteristics suggest
q: what does a hard lymph node mean
what does a left supraclavicular node mean
what does a tender node mean
what causes generalized lymphadenopathy
cards.x:
The feel of a lymph node in the neck tells you what kind of problem to suspect:

- Round or ovoid, smooth, mobile and non-tender: normal.
- Tender: inflammation.
- Hard or fixed: malignancy.
- Enlarged supraclavicular node on the left: metastasis from an abdominal or thoracic malignancy.
- Generalized: HIV, Epstein-Barr virus, lymphoma, leukemia or sarcoidosis.

The left supraclavicular node is the one worth knowing cold: it drains territory a long way from the neck, so finding one there redirects the entire search.

cards.t: Ludwig's angina
q: what is Ludwig's angina
why is Ludwig's angina an emergency
how does Ludwig's angina present
cards.x:
Ludwig's angina is a cellulitis (spreading skin and tissue infection) of the floor of the mouth. The signs are submandibular swelling and erythema, with early anterior neck edema. It is an infection of the lower mouth, usually from the teeth, and it spreads fast and downward.

It is life threatening, and the reason is the airway: the swelling can threaten breathing, so it is an emergency and has to be worked up quickly.

cards.t: The thyroid and trachea: what the exam findings suggest
q: what does a soft versus firm thyroid suggest
what causes a multinodular goiter
what causes tracheal deviation
where do you find the thyroid
cards.x:
Find the thyroid using the cricoid cartilage as the landmark. When the thyroid is diffusely enlarged, texture and tenderness give a first clue to which of three causes it is (blood tests then confirm it):

- Diffuse and soft: Graves disease.
- Diffuse and firm: Hashimoto thyroiditis.
- Diffuse and tender: thyroiditis.

Other patterns: endemic goiter means iodine deficiency; a single nodule is a cyst or tumor; multinodular enlargement is a metabolic process, with a risk of malignancy if there is a family history. Also check the trachea for deviation, which can come from masses, atelectasis (collapsed lung) or a large pneumothorax.

cards.t: Headache patterns in the head history
q: which headaches are unilateral
which headaches are episodic
what headache suggests subarachnoid hemorrhage
what does a new progressive headache suggest
cards.x:
The head history uses OPPQRST (onset, palliative, provoking, quality, radiation, site, timing) again, and the headache patterns matter:

- Migraine and tension headaches are episodic.
- Migraine and cluster headaches are unilateral. Migraine is in both lists, so the two features have to be read together.
- Sudden and severe: subarachnoid hemorrhage.
- New, progressive and persistent: a mass.

Also consider meningitis.

cards.t: The head examination: what to look for
q: what do you look for in the head exam
what does fine hair suggest
what does an enlarged head suggest
cards.x:
On examination of the head, look for facial swelling or distinctive facies; lumps, rashes, hair loss, lesions and scars; and lice. Fine hair suggests hyperthyroidism and coarse hair suggests hypothyroidism. Look for seborrheic dermatitis, psoriasis, atypical nevi and actinic keratosis.

Also check symmetry, involuntary movements and edema; tenderness and integrity; and size. The head is enlarged in hydrocephalus and Paget disease, and small in microcephaly.
